whyWrongByChoice.E: Refeeding syndrome is a complication of restoring nutrients, not a presenting growth pattern.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A public health officer reviews mortality data for children younger than 5 years in a region with chronic food deprivation. Approximately 45% of the deaths are linked to malnutrition. Which of the following is the most common proximate cause of death among these malnourished children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiac failure from heart muscle catabolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypoglycemia from impaired gluconeogenesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection with diarrhea and dehydration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal failure from calcium oxalate deposition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Starvation from complete caloric depletion

explanation.summary: Most malnutrition-linked deaths in children under 5 result from susceptibility to infection with diarrhea and dehydration, not starvation itself.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the 45% of deaths in children younger than 5 years that are linked to malnutrition, most children do not starve to death. Instead, chronic malnutrition makes them susceptible to infections, and they die from diarrhea and dehydration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heart muscle weakens in marasmus, but cardiac failure is not the stated leading cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fasting hypoglycemia is a consequence of chronic alcohol metabolism, not the leading cause of malnutrition deaths.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium oxalate renal failure is a feature of ethylene glycol poisoning, not malnutrition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most malnourished children do not actually starve to death; infection is the usual cause.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with severe marasmus is admitted to a hospital. Despite oral feeding, the child's weight continues to fall and stools contain poorly digested food. Which of the following best explains the failure of nutritional intake to reverse the child's condition at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low NAD+/NADH ratio inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased albumin lowers oncotic pressure and blocks nutrient uptake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deterioration of the digestive tract lining and degradation of enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Edema masks weight gain by shifting fluid into the tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral vasodilation diverts blood flow away from the intestine

explanation.summary: In end-stage marasmus, enzymes are degraded for energy and the digestive tract lining deteriorates, so food that is eaten cannot be absorbed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In marasmus, muscle and fat are oxidatively catabolized for energy and muscles from essential organ systems break down. In the end stages of disease, enzymes are in short supply because they are degraded and used for energy, and the digestive tract lining deteriorates so that what little food is eaten often cannot be absorbed. At this stage, mortality risk is extremely high without aggressive medical intervention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low NAD+/NADH ratio results from ethanol metabolism and is unrelated to this child's malabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low albumin and oncotic pressure cause edema in kwashiorkor; they are not the mechanism of malabsorption in marasmus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Edema is the distinguishing feature of kwashiorkor, not marasmus, and does not explain malabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peripheral vasodilation is an effect of alcohol, not a feature of marasmus.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl in a refugee camp has been eating adequate quantities of a carbohydrate-based staple with almost no protein for several months. Examination shows pitting edema of the legs, a distended abdomen, and hepatomegaly. Her weight for height is calculated to be within the normal range. Which of the following best explains the normal weight-for-height measurement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulated fluid in the extravascular space adds to body weight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth restriction lowers height proportionally with weight

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic glycogen stores expanded by carbohydrate intake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Muscle mass maintained by reduced protein catabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preservation of subcutaneous fat from adequate lipid intake

explanation.summary: In kwashiorkor, weight for height can be normal because accumulated edema fluid adds to body weight despite severe protein deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: This child has kwashiorkor, a specific lack of protein with otherwise adequate calories. Decreased albumin production lowers oncotic pressure, causing water to move from the intravascular into the extravascular space. This edema typically starts in the legs and is pronounced in the abdomen, and the accumulated fluid means weight for height can be normal even though the child is severely malnourished.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stunting is a feature of chronic malnutrition, and it does not explain the edema-related weight in kwashiorkor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen stores do not account for the weight; the accumulated fluid does.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein deficiency does not preserve muscle mass; the normal weight reflects fluid, not muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kwashiorkor is distinguished by edema, not by preserved fat; fat is not what normalizes the weight.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with kwashiorkor has a markedly enlarged liver on physical examination. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the hepatomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium oxalate crystals deposit within hepatic sinusoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased lipoprotein production impairs hepatic triglyceride secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen accumulates from a glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased albumin synthesis expands hepatocyte volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low oncotic pressure shifts fluid into the liver parenchyma

explanation.summary: Kwashiorkor hepatomegaly results from decreased lipoprotein production, which causes a defect in hepatic secretion of triglycerides.
explanation.whyCorrect: A physical exam of a child with kwashiorkor is often significant for hepatomegaly. The hepatomegaly associated with protein deficiency is due to a decrease in the production of lipoproteins, causing a defect in hepatic secretion of triglycerides, which then accumulate in the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium oxalate deposition occurs in the proximal renal tubule in ethylene glycol poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency is von Gierke's disease, not a feature of kwashiorkor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein deficiency decreases, not increases, hepatic albumin production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low oncotic pressure causes tissue edema; it does not explain the liver enlargement, which is due to retained triglycerides.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child from a war-torn region presents with broomstick extremities and loss of subcutaneous fat in the arms and legs, together with pitting edema of the lower legs and a distended abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic malnutrition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kwashiorkor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marasmic kwashiorkor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marasmus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Refeeding syndrome

explanation.summary: Marasmic kwashiorkor is the least common acute malnutrition state and combines the physical features of both marasmus and kwashiorkor.
explanation.whyCorrect: This child shows the wasting of marasmus (broomstick extremities, loss of subcutaneous fat) together with the edema that is the distinguishing feature of kwashiorkor. Marasmic kwashiorkor is a third acute malnutrition state that is the least common and combines the physical features of both marasmus and kwashiorkor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic malnutrition is characterized by stunting and decreased head circumference rather than acute wasting with edema.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kwashiorkor alone produces edema, and weight for height can be normal; broomstick extremities are not characteristic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marasmus alone produces wasting without edema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Refeeding syndrome is a complication of restoring nutrients, not the presenting malnutrition state.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pharmacologist explains to students that a particular medication is administered in a form that is pharmacologically inactive and must first be converted by metabolic pathways into the active agent. Which of the following terms best describes this medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzyme inducer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kinase substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pro-drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced coenzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic metabolite

explanation.summary: Pro-drugs are therapies given in a pharmacologically inactive form that metabolism converts into the active agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metabolism transforms molecules for ATP production, further use, and excretion or detoxification. The beneficial effects of metabolism can be capitalized upon in medicine: select therapies known as pro-drugs are administered in a form that is pharmacologically inactive and must first be converted by metabolic pathways into the active agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An enzyme inducer increases enzyme activity, as routine alcohol does to CYP2E1; it is not defined by requiring activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kinase substrates receive phosphoryl groups in substrate level phosphorylation; this does not describe an inactive drug form.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced coenzymes such as NADH carry electrons; they are not administered medications.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A toxic metabolite is a harmful product of metabolism, such as formic acid, not a deliberately inactive therapy.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man consumes several alcoholic beverages. In his liver, ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde and then further oxidized to acetate. Which of the following is the major fate of the acetate produced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excretion unchanged in the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidation to formic acid by CYP2E1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction back to acetaldehyde by ALDH

explanation.summary: Non-toxic acetate from ethanol oxidation is mainly transformed into acetyl-CoA for ATP production via the TCA cycle, with excretion only a minor route.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxidative catabolism of ethanol in the liver first produces acetaldehyde, and further oxidation yields non-toxic acetate. Acetate can be excreted, which is the minor route, or transformed into acetyl-CoA for ATP production via the TCA cycle, which is the major route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts pyruvate and lactate, not acetate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excretion of acetate is described as the minor route, not the major fate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Formic acid is a metabolite of methanol, not of ethanol-derived acetate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ALDH catalyzes the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate; it does not reverse the reaction.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies the minor pathways of ethanol oxidation in hepatocytes and isolates an enzyme that converts ethanol to acetaldehyde while reducing hydrogen peroxide to water. This enzyme metabolizes only a very small amount of alcohol. In which of the following cellular compartments is this enzyme located?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microsome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxisome

explanation.summary: Catalase, contained in peroxisomes, oxidizes a very small amount of ethanol to acetaldehyde using hydrogen peroxide.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first step of ethanol oxidation can occur three ways. Alcohol dehydrogenase in the cytosol is the major liver enzyme, CYP2E1 is enriched in hepatic microsomes, and catalase is contained in peroxisomes where it converts H2O2 to H2O while oxidizing ethanol. Catalase metabolizes only a very small amount of alcohol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cytosolic enzyme is alcohol dehydrogenase, which uses NAD+ and is the major route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The microsomal enzyme is CYP2E1, which uses NADPH and O2 rather than hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondria house acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which acts on acetaldehyde rather than ethanol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: None of the ethanol-oxidizing enzymes are described as nuclear.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with routine excessive alcohol consumption has markedly induced hepatic microsomal oxidation of ethanol. Which of the following sets of co-substrates is consumed by the induced microsomal enzyme as it converts ethanol to acetaldehyde?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NAD+, H+, and H2O

choices.label: B
choices.text: NAD+, H+, and O2

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADH, H+, and H2O2

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADP+, H+, and H2O2

choices.label: E
choices.text: NADPH, H+, and O2

explanation.summary: CYP2E1, the inducible microsomal ethanol oxidase, consumes NADPH, H+, and O2, producing NADP+ and water along with acetaldehyde.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytochrome P450 2E1 isoform is enriched in hepatic microsomes and is induced when alcohol consumption is excessive and routine. In the microsomal reaction, CYP2E1 converts ethanol to acetaldehyde while consuming NADPH + H+ + O2 and generating NADP+ + 2 H2O. This distinguishes it from alcohol dehydrogenase, which reduces NAD+ to NADH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NAD+ is the co-substrate of cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase, and water is a product of CYP2E1, not a reactant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAD+ with O2 does not describe either the ADH or the CYP2E1 reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither NADH nor H2O2 is consumed by CYP2E1; H2O2 is the co-substrate of peroxisomal catalase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADP+ is the product of the CYP2E1 reaction, and H2O2 is used by catalase in peroxisomes.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher fractionates hepatocytes into cytosolic, microsomal, peroxisomal, and mitochondrial components and measures the NAD+-dependent conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate in each fraction. In which of the following fractions is this activity expected to be greatest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microsome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peroxisome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma membrane

explanation.summary: Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate within mitochondria, reducing NAD+ to NADH.
explanation.whyCorrect: While the first step of ethanol oxidation can occur by three routes, the final oxidative step is catalyzed only by a member of the aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) family. Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate in the mitochondria while reducing NAD+ to NADH. This is why ethanol oxidation through ADH and ALDH causes NADH to accumulate both in the cytosol and in the mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cytosol houses alcohol dehydrogenase, which acts on ethanol rather than acetaldehyde.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microsomes contain CYP2E1, which oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, not acetaldehyde to acetate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peroxisomes contain catalase, which metabolizes only a small amount of ethanol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: None of the ethanol-oxidizing enzymes are described as plasma membrane enzymes.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with chronic habitual alcohol abuse is found to have a fatty liver on abdominal imaging. Which of the following best explains the accumulation of lipid in his liver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low NAD+/NADH ratio inhibits hepatic lipid metabolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetaldehyde directly stimulates hepatic lipoprotein secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased protein intake reduces hepatic albumin production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated NAD+ accelerates hepatic lipid oxidation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Induction of CYP2E1 increases hepatic triglyceride synthesis

explanation.summary: Ethanol oxidation lowers the NAD+/NADH ratio, which inhibits hepatic lipid metabolism and produces a fatty liver in chronic alcoholics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ethanol oxidation through ADH and ALDH causes accumulation of NADH in the cytosol and mitochondria. Because the liver predominantly metabolizes ethanol, hepatic metabolic processes are particularly disrupted. Both lipid metabolism and gluconeogenesis are inhibited by the low NAD+/NADH ratio caused by ethanol metabolism, which accounts for why chronic alcoholics can present with a fatty liver and fasting hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetaldehyde is a toxic intermediate responsible for hangover symptoms; it is not described as stimulating lipoprotein secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced albumin from protein deficiency causes edema in kwashiorkor; it is not the mechanism of alcoholic fatty liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ethanol metabolism lowers NAD+ relative to NADH; NAD+ is not elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CYP2E1 induction is relevant to acetaminophen poisoning and porphyria, not to increased triglyceride synthesis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man stranded outdoors in extreme cold drinks alcohol, believing it will protect him against hypothermia. He feels warmer in his hands and face, but his core body temperature continues to fall. Which of the following best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaldehyde stimulates shivering in skeletal muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol consolidates blood flow to the core and vital organs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ethanol oxidation releases heat that warms vital organs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased NADH raises the metabolic rate of the core

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral vasodilation shifts blood flow away from the core

explanation.summary: Alcohol induces peripheral vasodilation that warms the periphery at the expense of keeping the core and vital organs warm.
explanation.whyCorrect: A dangerous misunderstanding is that alcohol warms the body or protects against hypothermia. Alcohol induces vasodilation within the periphery to increase blood flow, which brings added warmth to the periphery but at the expense of keeping the bodily core and vital organs warm. This counteracts the body's natural response of consolidating blood flow to the core in extreme cold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaldehyde accounts for hangover symptoms; it does not drive protective shivering.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the body's natural cold response, which alcohol counteracts rather than promotes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The perceived warmth comes from redistributed blood flow, not from heat generated by ethanol oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADH accumulation disrupts hepatic metabolism; it does not raise core metabolic rate.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops headache, severe nausea, and visual disturbances after drinking improperly distilled liquor contaminated with methanol. Which of the following is the direct product of alcohol dehydrogenase acting on methanol?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaldehyde

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formaldehyde

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycolaldehyde

explanation.summary: Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde, which ALDH then converts to formic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methanol is metabolized by ADH into formaldehyde, and formaldehyde is then metabolized by ALDH into formic acid. Methanol and ethanol are acted upon by the same set of dehydrogenases because chemically similar substrates can be catalyzed by the same enzyme. The metabolites of methanol account for all of its toxic effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaldehyde is the ADH product of ethanol, not methanol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetate is the non-toxic final product of ethanol oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Formic acid is produced from formaldehyde by ALDH, the second step, not the first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycolaldehyde is the ADH product of ethylene glycol.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A hiker is stung by a wasp while far from medical care. A companion applies smokeless tobacco to the sting site, and the pain and local reaction diminish. Which of the following best explains the benefit of this remedy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nicotine induces CYP2E1 to metabolize the venom

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nicotine inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase in the skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotine is a base that neutralizes injected formic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tobacco adsorbs oxalic acid injected by the insect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tobacco constricts peripheral vessels to limit venom spread

explanation.summary: Much of the pain from bee, ant, and wasp stings is due to injected formic acid, which nicotine, a base, can neutralize.
explanation.whyCorrect: Formic acid has a spectrum of adverse physiological effects. A great deal of the pain and reaction associated with bee, ant, and wasp stings is attributed to formic acid injected during the bite or sting. Nicotine is a base that can neutralize the formic acid and dampen its impact, which is why applying tobacco is a quick remedy when standard treatment is unavailable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2E1 induction by chronic alcohol is relevant to acetaminophen poisoning, not to insect venom.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ALDH is a hepatic enzyme of alcohol metabolism and is not the target of this remedy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insect stings inject formic acid; oxalic acid is the toxic product of ethylene glycol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The remedy works by chemical neutralization, not by vasoconstriction.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with flank pain and is found to have numerous folded envelope-shaped crystals in her urine. She denies any ingestion of antifreeze or other household chemicals, and her anion gap is normal. She reports taking very large doses of a dietary supplement for the past year. Excess of which of the following best accounts for her crystals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin D

explanation.summary: Calcium oxalate stones can result from other metabolic issues such as excess vitamin D, not only from ethylene glycol poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folded envelope-shaped crystals are the hallmark of calcium oxalate. Although calcium oxalate crystals precipitating in the proximal renal tubule are a feature of ethylene glycol ingestion, they can also be caused by other metabolic issues, such as excess vitamin D. The absence of any toxic ingestion and a normal anion gap point toward this alternative cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate is not linked to calcium oxalate precipitation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron excess is not described as a cause of calcium oxalate crystal formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin B12 is not linked to calcium oxalate precipitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C excess is not the cause of calcium oxalate stones identified in this context.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical student calculates a patient's anion gap using the formula AG = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) and asks why potassium is excluded even though it is a measured serum cation. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Potassium cannot be measured on a basic metabolic panel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potassium does not participate in maintaining serum neutrality

choices.label: C
choices.text: Potassium is an anion already accounted for by chloride

choices.label: D
choices.text: Potassium is entirely intracellular and absent from serum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Potassium's low concentration minimally alters the result

explanation.summary: Potassium is commonly omitted from the anion gap because its serum concentration is significantly lower than the other variables and its inclusion minimally alters the formula.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some versions of the anion gap formula consider the contribution of K+, but because this ion has a concentration that is significantly below the other variables and its inclusion minimally alters the formula, a common practice is to simplify the calculation by excluding K+. The formula uses Na+, Cl-, and bicarbonate because they are the most easily measured ions that adjust concentration to maintain serum neutrality.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Potassium is routinely reported on a basic metabolic panel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All serum ions contribute to neutrality; potassium is excluded for its small magnitude, not for lack of participation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potassium is a cation, not an anion, and is not represented by chloride.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium is present and measured in serum (for example, 4.0 mEq/L on a basic metabolic panel).

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe chronic malnutrition and a markedly low serum albumin has a calculated anion gap of 4 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains this low anion gap?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of unmeasured anions such as lactate and ketoacids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of bicarbonate as a buffer for excess circulating protons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased serum sodium from extravascular fluid shifts in hypoalbuminemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated serum potassium that was omitted from the calculated formula

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of anionic proteins with a compensatory rise in serum chloride

explanation.summary: A low anion gap indicates loss of unmeasured anions such as albumin, with chloride rising to maintain serum neutrality.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anion gap reflects contributions from unmeasured sources. A high anion gap suggests increased levels of unmeasured ions, while a low anion gap is indicative of a loss of unmeasured anions such as anionic proteins like albumin. Because serum is always chemically neutral, the loss of anionic charge is usually offset by a compensatory rise in chloride ions, which narrows the calculated gap.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulation of unmeasured anions like lactic acid raises the anion gap rather than lowering it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bicarbonate consumption by acid accompanies a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, not a low gap.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The low gap here reflects a compensatory chloride rise, not a primary sodium loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium is excluded because it minimally alters the formula; it does not explain a gap of 4 mEq/L.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea has the following serum values: Na+ 140 mEq/L, Cl- 110 mEq/L, and HCO3- 18 mEq/L. Her serum pH is 7.30. Which of the following best characterizes her acid-base disturbance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis from lactic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis from toxic alcohol ingestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low anion gap from loss of unmeasured anions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory acidosis with a normal anion gap

explanation.summary: Metabolic acidosis can occur with a normal anion gap, as in diarrhea; here AG = 140 - (110 + 18) = 12 mEq/L, within the normal 8-16 range.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acidosis (pH below 7.4) with bicarbonate below the normal 22-29 mEq/L range indicates a metabolic acidosis. Calculating the anion gap gives 140 - (110 + 18) = 12 mEq/L, which falls within the normal ~8-16 mEq/L range. Metabolic acidosis can occur with an anion gap within normal ranges, and diarrhea is the example given, in contrast to the high anion gap seen with toxic alcohol metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactic acid accumulation would raise the anion gap above the normal range.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic alcohols produce a high anion gap; this patient's gap of 12 is normal and there is no ingestion history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A gap of 12 mEq/L is within normal limits, not low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The low bicarbonate and low pH indicate a metabolic, not respiratory, basis for the acidosis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man ingests methanol. Twelve hours later, his serum bicarbonate is 9 mEq/L (normal 22-29 mEq/L) and his anion gap is 30 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the relationship between his low bicarbonate and elevated anion gap?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bicarbonate moves into cells, and potassium replaces it as the serum anion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complex IV inhibition consumes bicarbonate, leaving sodium unbalanced in the serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formic acid blocks renal bicarbonate synthesis, and chloride falls to compensate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protons from formic acid consume bicarbonate, and the deprotonated acid adds an unmeasured anion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal bicarbonate excretion rises in exchange for chloride, widening the gap

explanation.summary: Toxic acids donate protons that are buffered by bicarbonate, and the resulting negatively charged anions are unmeasured, so bicarbonate falls as the anion gap rises.
explanation.whyCorrect: The acids produced from toxic alcohol metabolism donate protons to decrease bodily pH. As the acids donate protons, they become negatively charged anions contributing to the gap. The increase in additional anions is typically at the expense of bicarbonate because bicarbonate is a conjugate base released by the kidneys to provide buffering capacity when systemic proton concentration increases. This is why both pH and bicarbonate are low in a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Potassium is a cation, not an anion, and its serum change does not explain the widened gap.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Formic acid inhibits complex IV to blunt ATP formation; this does not consume serum bicarbonate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A compensatory chloride change relates to a low anion gap; here the gap is high because of unmeasured acid anions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bicarbonate falls because it is consumed as a buffer, not because the kidneys excrete it; the kidneys release bicarbonate to buffer.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is treated for ethylene glycol poisoning. His high anion gap metabolic acidosis is attributed not only to the acidic end products of ethylene glycol oxidation but also to a second acid. Which of the following best explains the source of this second acid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium oxalate crystals release protons as they precipitate in the renal tubule

choices.label: B
choices.text: CYP2E1 induction produces hydrogen peroxide that acidifies the serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycolaldehyde is converted to acetate, which is then oxidized to acetic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADH generated by ADH and ALDH drives conversion of pyruvate to lactic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxalic acid inhibits complex IV, causing bicarbonate consumption in mitochondria

explanation.summary: Oxidation of toxic alcohols by ADH and ALDH raises NADH, shifting the LDH equilibrium toward lactic acid, which adds to the acidosis alongside the alcohol's own acidic products.
explanation.whyCorrect: The end products of toxic alcohol metabolism yield acids (glyoxylic and oxalic acid for ethylene glycol). In addition, oxidative conversion of these alcohols occurs via ADH and ALDH, which increases NADH levels. The elevated NADH favors lactic acid formation from pyruvate through the reversible LDH reaction, so lactic acid also contributes to the metabolic acidosis with high anion gap.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium oxalate precipitation causes renal failure; it is not described as a proton source.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP2E1 uses NADPH and O2 and produces water; it is not a source of serum acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycolaldehyde is oxidized by ALDH to glyoxylic acid, not to acetate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complex IV inhibition is the effect of formic acid in methanol poisoning, not a source of acid in ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview I: General Reactions (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company develops a novel type 2 diabetes drug that binds a gluconeogenic enzyme to suppress hepatic glucose production. For the drug to reach its target enzyme, in which cellular locale must the majority of gluconeogenesis be occurring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitochondrial intermembrane space

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxisome

explanation.summary: Gluconeogenesis occurs predominantly in the cytosol of hepatocytes, so a drug targeting a gluconeogenic enzyme must be present there.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although gluconeogenesis spans several compartments (pyruvate carboxylase in the mitochondria and glucose 6-phosphatase in the endoplasmic reticulum), the majority of its enzymatic steps are cytosolic. A drug that must bind a gluconeogenic enzyme to suppress hepatic glucose output must therefore be present in the cytosol where most of the pathway operates.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The intermembrane space is a proton reservoir for OXPHOS and does not house gluconeogenic enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only a single gluconeogenic step (pyruvate carboxylase) is in the matrix; the bulk of the pathway is cytosolic, so the matrix alone would not allow the drug to work.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleus houses DNA-related processes and is not a site of gluconeogenic carbon flux.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peroxisomes participate in very-long-chain fatty acid catabolism, not gluconeogenesis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: In a cell, acetyl-CoA is oxidatively catabolized to carbon dioxide with the generation of reduced coenzymes (NADH, FADH2) that then feed the electron transport chain. Which pathway is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-oxidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gluconeogenesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: TCA cycle

explanation.summary: The TCA cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA to produce reduced coenzymes that fuel the ETC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The TCA cycle, located in the mitochondrial matrix, oxidizes acetyl-CoA predominantly to produce reduced coenzymes (NADH and FADH2) plus some ATP, providing reduction potential to the ETC for ATP production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA from fatty acids rather than consuming it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gluconeogenesis is a reductive, anabolic pathway that makes glucose and does not consume acetyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycolysis oxidizes glucose to pyruvate and never uses acetyl-CoA as a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pentose phosphate pathway processes glycolytic intermediates to make NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate, not acetyl-CoA.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A biochemistry student traces electrons donated by NADH as they travel through the electron transport chain to their terminal acceptor. Which sequence correctly represents this path?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complex I -> coenzyme Q -> complex II -> cytochrome c -> complex III -> complex IV -> O2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complex I -> coenzyme Q -> complex III -> cytochrome c -> complex IV -> O2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complex I -> complex II -> complex III -> complex IV -> coenzyme Q -> O2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complex I -> cytochrome c -> complex III -> coenzyme Q -> complex IV -> O2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complex II -> coenzyme Q -> complex III -> cytochrome c -> complex IV -> O2

explanation.summary: NADH-derived electrons enter at complex I, are shuttled by coenzyme Q to complex III, then by cytochrome c to complex IV, and finally to oxygen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the electrons are donated by NADH, flow begins at complex I. From complex I, coenzyme Q shuttles the electrons to complex III, then cytochrome c carries them to complex IV, which passes them to O2 as the terminal acceptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NADH-derived electrons pass from complex I directly to complex III via coenzyme Q and do not route through complex II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxygen is the terminal acceptor at complex IV, so coenzyme Q cannot come after complex IV, and NADH electrons bypass complex II.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lipid-soluble shuttles are in the wrong order; coenzyme Q acts before complex III and cytochrome c after it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Electrons from NADH enter at complex I; complex II is the entry point for FADH2, not NADH.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A researcher inserts pH-sensitive probes into the intermembrane space and the matrix of an actively respiring, healthy mitochondrion. How does the pH of the intermembrane space compare to that of the matrix, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Higher, because of a higher concentration of protons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher, because of a lower concentration of protons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Identical, because protons freely equilibrate across the inner membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower, because of a higher concentration of protons

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower, because of a lower concentration of protons

explanation.summary: The ETC pumps protons into the intermembrane space, raising proton concentration and lowering pH there relative to the matrix.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ETC translocates protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, enriching it with protons. Because pH equals -log[H+], a higher proton concentration means a lower pH, so the intermembrane space is more acidic than the matrix.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A higher proton concentration lowers pH; it cannot raise it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The intermembrane space has more protons, not fewer, and its pH is lower rather than higher.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protons are charged and cannot freely cross the lipid inner membrane, which is exactly why the gradient can be maintained.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The proton concentration is higher, not lower, in the intermembrane space.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: Oxidative phosphorylation is described as the functional coupling of two distinct processes. Which pair of processes is coupled during OXPHOS?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP synthase and cytosolic lactate production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-oxidation and cytosolic glycolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytosolic glycolysis and the mitochondrial TCA cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ketone body formation and mitochondrial beta-oxidation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase

explanation.summary: OXPHOS couples the ETC, which builds the proton gradient, to ATP synthase, which uses that gradient to make ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ETC establishes the proton gradient, and ATP synthase is fully dependent on the flow of protons through it to catalyze ATP production. This functional dependence makes the two processes coupled during OXPHOS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactate production typically rises when ATP synthase is not functioning optimally; the two are not coupled.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-oxidation and glycolysis are independent pathways that oxidize different substrates in different locales.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycolysis can supply acetyl-CoA to the TCA cycle, but the two are not coupled in the OXPHOS sense.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heightened beta-oxidation can lead to ketone body formation, but these are linked, not coupled.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A patient ingests a toxin that renders the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. Which set of consequences best describes the effect on oxidative phosphorylation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycolysis in the cytosol is directly blocked at phosphofructokinase-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxygen consumption ceases entirely while ATP production continues unaffected

choices.label: C
choices.text: The electron transport chain stops completely but ATP synthase continues to make ATP normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proton gradient dissipates, ATP synthesis falls, and energy is released as heat

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proton gradient strengthens and ATP synthesis increases several-fold

explanation.summary: Uncoupling lets protons bypass ATP synthase, collapsing the gradient so its energy is dissipated as heat instead of captured as ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: ATP synthase depends on protons flowing through it. If protons instead leak across the inner membrane by an alternate route, the ETC and ATP synthase are uncoupled: the gradient dissipates, ATP synthesis drops, and the energy that would have driven ATP production is released as heat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uncouplers act on the mitochondrial inner membrane and do not directly block cytosolic glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uncoupling actually tends to accelerate electron flow and oxygen consumption while ATP output falls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ATP synthase requires the proton gradient; if protons bypass it, it cannot continue making ATP normally.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allowing protons to leak dissipates rather than strengthens the gradient, decreasing ATP synthesis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant has hypotonia, seizures, and markedly elevated serum very-long-chain fatty acids, consistent with a peroxisomal disorder (Zellweger spectrum). The very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate because catabolism that normally occurs in which organelle is defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxisome

explanation.summary: Very-long-chain fatty acids are handled by peroxisomal beta-oxidation, so peroxisomal disorders cause them to accumulate.
explanation.whyCorrect: While most beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, very-long-chain fatty acids are catabolized in the peroxisome. Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger spectrum disorder impair this contribution to long-chain fatty acid catabolism, so these fatty acids accumulate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cytosol hosts glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, not fatty acid beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endoplasmic reticulum participates in steps such as glucose 6-phosphatase activity, not very-long-chain fatty acid catabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysosomal defects cause storage diseases from failed turnover of cellular constituents, not the very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mitochondrial matrix handles standard-length fatty acids; very-long-chain species require the peroxisome.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A cell rapidly synthesizing fatty acids and nucleic acids upregulates a cytosolic pathway to supply reducing equivalents and a five-carbon sugar. Which pathway is this, and what are its principal products?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-oxidation; acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2 in the matrix

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gluconeogenesis; glucose 6-phosphate and free glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycolysis; cytosolic pyruvate, lactate, and net ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pentose phosphate pathway; NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: TCA cycle; matrix NADH, FADH2, and GTP per turn

explanation.summary: The pentose phosphate pathway is a cytosolic shunt of glycolysis that produces NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pentose phosphate pathway shunts glycolytic intermediates to generate NADPH (reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis and neutralizing oxidative species) and ribose 5-phosphate (the five-carbon sugar for RNA and DNA), matching the cell's needs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA and reduced coenzymes from fatty acids, not NADPH or ribose 5-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gluconeogenesis produces glucose, not the reducing equivalents and sugar the cell needs here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycolysis yields pyruvate/lactate and does not supply NADPH or ribose 5-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TCA cycle produces NADH and FADH2 in the matrix, not NADPH or ribose sugar, and is not cytosolic.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: During a prolonged fast, a patient's hepatocytes undergo heightened beta-oxidation of fatty acids and begin producing ketone bodies. In which specific cellular location does this ketone body synthesis occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol of hepatocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix of skeletal muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxisome of hepatocytes

explanation.summary: Ketogenesis occurs in the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes during periods of heightened fatty acid beta-oxidation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ketone body formation predominantly occurs in the liver, and during times of heightened beta-oxidation of fatty acids, ketogenesis takes place within the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cytosol hosts glycolysis and much of gluconeogenesis, not ketogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endoplasmic reticulum is not where ketone bodies are produced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ketogenesis occurs predominantly in the liver; skeletal muscle uses ketone bodies rather than making them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The peroxisome catabolizes very-long-chain fatty acids but is not the site of ketone body synthesis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: Under severe cellular stress, cytochrome c is released from the mitochondria into the cytosol, where it triggers a cascade that activates caspases. This event initiates which process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaerobic glycolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apoptosis (programmed cell death)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gluconeogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased ATP synthesis by ATP synthase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ketone body formation

explanation.summary: Cytosolic cytochrome c activates caspases, initiating apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The release of cytochrome c from the ETC into the cytosol initiates a series of reactions culminating in the activation of caspases, the enzymes critical for apoptotic induction, so this event triggers apoptosis, or programmed cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaerobic glycolysis is a cytosolic energy pathway and is not triggered by caspase activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gluconeogenesis is glucose synthesis and is unrelated to cytochrome c release or caspase activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of cytochrome c from the ETC impairs electron transport and thus reduces, rather than increases, ATP synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ketone body formation results from heightened beta-oxidation, not from cytosolic cytochrome c.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: Electrons carried by FADH2 enter the electron transport chain at a different point than those carried by NADH. At which complex do FADH2-derived electrons enter the chain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP synthase (Complex V)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complex I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complex II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complex III

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complex IV

explanation.summary: FADH2 donates its electrons to complex II, whereas NADH donates at complex I.
explanation.whyCorrect: NADH-derived electrons enter the ETC at complex I, while FADH2 donates its electrons to complex II. From complex II the electrons are passed to coenzyme Q and onward through complex III, cytochrome c, and complex IV to oxygen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP synthase does not participate directly in electron transfer and is not an electron entry point.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complex I is the entry point for electrons from NADH, not FADH2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complex III receives electrons from coenzyme Q, downstream of the entry complexes, not directly from FADH2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complex IV is the terminal complex that passes electrons to oxygen, not an entry point.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A mutation causes a hepatocyte's mitochondria to form with markedly fewer cristae than normal. Assuming other components are intact, which consequence is most likely, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A shift of glycolysis into the mitochondria to compensate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased ATP production due to a larger matrix volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the TCA cycle because cristae contain its enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change in ATP production because cristae do not affect OXPHOS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced ATP production due to a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio

explanation.summary: Cristae expand inner-membrane surface area for OXPHOS machinery, so fewer cristae lower ATP output.
explanation.whyCorrect: The OXPHOS machinery is expressed on the inner mitochondrial membrane, so ATP production is limited by the abundance of that membrane. Cristae maximize the surface-area-to-volume ratio, augmenting OXPHOS. With fewer cristae, there is less inner-membrane surface to house the ETC and ATP synthase, reducing ATP production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycolysis is cytosolic and does not relocate into the mitochondria to compensate for lost cristae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A larger matrix volume without added inner membrane does not raise ATP output; the limiting factor is inner-membrane surface area.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TCA cycle enzymes reside in the matrix, not on the cristae, so the cycle is not lost.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cristae directly affect OXPHOS capacity by increasing inner-membrane surface area, so their loss does matter.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A cell biologist studies why eukaryotic cells confine the enzymes, substrates, and products of a given metabolic pathway to a single organelle. Which of the following best describes an advantage of this compartmentalization?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elimination of the need for energy input

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free diffusion of reactive intermediates through the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolation of the reactions from competing processes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower reaction yield in exchange for safety

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced need for regulation of the pathway

explanation.summary: Compartmentalization increases the fidelity of metabolic reactions by placing substrates, enzymes, and products in close proximity while isolating them from competing processes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Compartmentalization of metabolic pathways is critical for containment and sequestration of reactive metabolites, proper regulation of the pathways, and maximizing reaction yield. Localizing substrates, enzymes, and products within close physical proximity while concomitantly isolating those reactions from competing processes increases the fidelity of the reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sequestering a pathway does not eliminate energy requirements; establishing gradients and driving synthesis still require energy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A key purpose of compartmentalization is the containment of reactive metabolites, not their free diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Compartmentalization maximizes reaction yield rather than sacrificing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Compartmentalization supports proper regulation of pathways; it does not remove the need for it.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A researcher is mapping which metabolic pathways share a cellular compartment with glycolysis. Which of the following pathways occurs in the same cellular locale as glycolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electron transport chain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen degradation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ketogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: TCA cycle

explanation.summary: Glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and glycogen synthesis/degradation all occur in the cytosol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytosol houses glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and glycogen synthesis and degradation. In contrast, fatty acid beta-oxidation, the TCA cycle, and the components of OXPHOS (the ETC and ATP synthase) are housed within the mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (and peroxisome for very long chain fatty acids), not the cytosol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ETC is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ketogenesis occurs within the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TCA cycle is located in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A hepatologist explains that a single pathway in hepatocytes requires enzymes housed in several different compartments because of differences in enzyme expression and organelle localization. In which combination of compartments does hepatic gluconeogenesis take place?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosol and peroxisome, with no mitochondrial step

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytosol only, with no mitochondrial involvement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytosol, mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytosol, nucleus, and lysosome, but not mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitochondria and lysosome, with no cytosolic step

explanation.summary: Gluconeogenesis spans the cytosol (majority), mitochondria (pyruvate carboxylase), and endoplasmic reticulum (glucose 6-phosphatase).
explanation.whyCorrect: Gluconeogenesis occurs primarily in hepatocytes and spans multiple cellular compartments. The majority of the pathway is cytosolic, but pyruvate carboxylase resides in the mitochondria and glucose 6-phosphatase resides in the endoplasmic reticulum, so all three compartments participate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The peroxisome contributes to very long chain fatty acid catabolism, not gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although most gluconeogenic steps are cytosolic, pyruvate carboxylase and glucose 6-phosphatase reside in other organelles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither the nucleus nor the lysosome participates in gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lysosome is not involved in gluconeogenesis, and the cytosol houses the majority of the pathway.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has been fasting for 36 hours. His liver is actively producing glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors. Which of the following is a carbon source used by hepatic gluconeogenesis in this state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free fatty acids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycerol released by lipolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADPH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribose 5-phosphate

explanation.summary: Gluconeogenic substrates are pyruvate derived from sources such as alanine and lactate, or glycerol from lipolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gluconeogenesis produces glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors in times of fasting. Its substrates are pyruvate derived from a variety of sources (e.g., alanine, lactate) or glycerol formed from lipolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA is the product of beta-oxidation and the substrate of the TCA cycle; it is not listed as a gluconeogenic substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty acids are the substrate of beta-oxidation; only the glycerol released by lipolysis feeds gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH is a reducing equivalent produced by the pentose phosphate pathway, not a carbon source for glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ribose 5-phosphate is a product of the pentose phosphate pathway used for RNA and DNA, not a gluconeogenic substrate.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A hepatocyte is analyzed during a period of high energy demand. Which of the following changes would be expected to increase the rate of hepatic glycolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased insulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated alanine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated AMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated glucagon

choices.label: E
choices.text: High ATP/ADP ratio

explanation.summary: In the liver, glycolysis is stimulated by insulin and AMP and inhibited by glucagon, alanine, and a high ATP/ADP ratio.
explanation.whyCorrect: The major regulators of hepatic glycolysis are insulin (+), glucagon (-), alanine (-), AMP (+), and a high ATP/ADP ratio (-). Rising AMP signals low energy charge and stimulates glycolysis to generate ATP and pyruvate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin is a positive regulator of glycolysis, so decreased insulin would reduce, not increase, glycolytic rate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alanine inhibits hepatic glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucagon is a negative regulator of hepatic glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A high ATP/ADP ratio signals energy sufficiency and inhibits glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sprinter's skeletal muscle becomes transiently oxygen-limited during a 400-meter race, and her muscle cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis. Which set of products is generated by glycolysis under these conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose, NADPH, and ribose 5-phosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactate, ATP, and NAD+

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactate, FADH2, and CO2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate, ATP, and NADH

explanation.summary: Anaerobic glycolysis yields lactate, ATP, and regenerated NAD+, whereas aerobic glycolysis yields pyruvate, ATP, and NADH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycolysis uses glucose and NAD+ as substrates. Under aerobic conditions its general products are pyruvate, ATP, and NADH; under anaerobic conditions the products are lactate, ATP, and NAD+, with the regenerated NAD+ allowing glycolysis to continue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2 are the products of beta-oxidation, not glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate are pentose phosphate pathway products, and glucose is a product of gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycolysis does not generate FADH2, and CO2 is produced by the TCA cycle rather than by glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate, ATP, and NADH are the products of aerobic, not anaerobic, glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A quiescent cell has accumulated abundant reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis. Which of the following would most directly decrease flux through the pentose phosphate pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated glucagon

choices.label: B
choices.text: High acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio

choices.label: C
choices.text: High ATP/ADP ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: High NADH/NAD+ ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: High NADPH/NADP+ ratio

explanation.summary: The pentose phosphate pathway is negatively regulated by a high NADPH/NADP+ ratio.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pentose phosphate pathway shunts glycolytic intermediates to produce NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate. Its major regulator is the NADPH/NADP+ ratio; when NADPH is abundant, the high ratio inhibits the pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucagon regulates hepatic glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, not the pentose phosphate pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio is a negative regulator of beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A high ATP/ADP ratio regulates glycolysis and ETC/OXPHOS, not the pentose phosphate pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A high NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits beta-oxidation and the TCA cycle, not the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: In a hepatocyte, the TCA cycle slows and the two-carbon unit that feeds it accumulates in the mitochondrial matrix. Which of the following ratio changes would be expected to inhibit beta-oxidation in this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio

choices.label: B
choices.text: High AMP/ATP ratio

choices.label: C
choices.text: High insulin/glucagon ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: High NAD+/NADH ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: High NADPH/NADP+ ratio

explanation.summary: Beta-oxidation is inhibited by a high NADH/NAD+ ratio and a high acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2 from fatty acids. Its major regulators are the NADH/NAD+ ratio and the acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio; when acetyl-CoA accumulates, the high acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio feeds back to inhibit further beta-oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: AMP is a positive regulator of hepatic glycolysis and is not listed as a regulator of beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin and glucagon regulate glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver, not beta-oxidation directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A high NAD+/NADH ratio favors beta-oxidation; it is the high NADH/NAD+ ratio that inhibits it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The NADPH/NADP+ ratio regulates the pentose phosphate pathway, not beta-oxidation.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A biochemist measures TCA cycle flux in isolated mitochondria while manipulating the matrix environment. Which of the following changes would most directly decrease flux through the TCA cycle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fall in the ATP/ADP ratio

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rise in acetyl-CoA availability

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rise in FAD availability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rise in the NAD+/NADH ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rise in the NADH/NAD+ ratio

explanation.summary: The TCA cycle requires NAD+ and FAD as substrates and is inhibited by a high NADH/NAD+ ratio.
explanation.whyCorrect: The TCA cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA using NAD+ and FAD as co-substrates to produce NADH, FADH2, and ATP. Its major regulator is the NADH/NAD+ ratio; a high ratio indicates the ETC is not consuming NADH fast enough, and it inhibits the cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A falling ATP/ADP ratio signals energy demand and would not inhibit the cycle; the table lists NADH/NAD+ as the TCA regulator.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetyl-CoA is the substrate of the TCA cycle; increased availability would not decrease flux.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FAD is a required substrate; increased availability supports rather than inhibits the cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A rise in NAD+/NADH means more oxidized substrate is available and would favor, not inhibit, the cycle.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A resting skeletal muscle cell has a high ATP/ADP ratio. Which of the following best describes the effect of this state on the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased flux through the ETC and OXPHOS

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased ATP synthesis to build energy stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased proton pumping with unchanged ATP synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change, because OXPHOS is regulated only by oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncoupling of the ETC from ATP synthase

explanation.summary: A high ATP/ADP ratio is the major negative regulator of ETC/OXPHOS.
explanation.whyCorrect: ETC/OXPHOS produces energy from the reduced coenzyme electron carriers NADH and FADH2. Its major regulator is the ATP/ADP ratio; when ATP is abundant relative to ADP, flux through the ETC and OXPHOS decreases, matching ATP production to cellular demand.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A high ATP/ADP ratio signals that ATP is already sufficient and inhibits rather than stimulates ATP synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proton pumping and ATP synthesis are coupled; a high ATP/ADP ratio reduces both rather than increasing pumping alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxygen is a substrate of the ETC, but the ATP/ADP ratio is a major regulator of OXPHOS flux.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncoupling occurs when protons bypass ATP synthase; a high ATP/ADP ratio does not uncouple the processes.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: In a tissue in which oxidative phosphorylation has been uncoupled by natural means, electrons continue to flow through the electron transport chain. Which of the following products continues to be formed by the ETC in this uncoupled state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: H2O

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactate

choices.label: E
choices.text: NADH

explanation.summary: Coupled ETC/OXPHOS produces ATP and H2O; uncoupled ETC produces heat and H2O.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ETC uses O2, NADH, and FADH2 as substrates. When coupled to ATP synthase, its general products are ATP and H2O; when uncoupled, the products are heat and H2O. Water is formed either way because electrons are still ultimately transferred to oxygen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is produced only when the ETC is coupled to ATP synthase; in the uncoupled state the energy is released as heat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose is the product of gluconeogenesis, not of the ETC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactate is a product of anaerobic glycolysis, not of the ETC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NADH is a substrate consumed by the ETC, not a product of it.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A lipid-soluble molecule shuttles electrons within the inner mitochondrial membrane from complex I or complex II to complex III. By which of the following names is this shuttle also known?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complex V

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytochrome c

choices.label: C
choices.text: FAD

choices.label: D
choices.text: NAD+

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ubiquinone

explanation.summary: Coenzyme Q, also referred to as ubiquinone, is a lipid-soluble electron shuttle of the ETC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ETC passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 through protein complexes and two lipid-soluble shuttles: coenzyme Q (CoQ, also referred to as ubiquinone) and cytochrome c. CoQ carries electrons from complex I or complex II to complex III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complex V is ATP synthase, which does not participate directly in electron transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome c is the other lipid-soluble shuttle, carrying electrons from complex III to complex IV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FAD is the oxidized form of the reduced coenzyme FADH2, which donates electrons to complex II; it is not the shuttle to complex III.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAD+ is the oxidized form of NADH, which donates electrons to complex I.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A student proposes that mitochondria use ATP hydrolysis as the energy source to pump protons into the intermembrane space. Which of the following best explains why this proposal is incorrect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP synthase running in reverse builds the gradient using NADH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electron flow through the ETC supplies the energy, so no ATP is consumed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxygen reduction at complex I alone drives all proton pumping

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protons spontaneously concentrate in the intermembrane space without energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The TCA cycle pumps protons directly across the inner membrane

explanation.summary: Because ATP production is the goal of OXPHOS, spending ATP to build the proton gradient would be futile; the ETC provides the energy instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gradients naturally dissipate, so establishing one requires energy. Using ATP to establish the proton gradient would be futile since ATP production is the goal of OXPHOS. The ETC provides an alternative energy source by obtaining electrons from NADH and FADH2 and passing them through the complexes; as electrons flow, the proton gradient is generated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP synthase does not participate directly in electron transfer and does not use NADH; the ETC complexes build the gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxygen is the terminal acceptor at complex IV, not complex I, and the gradient is generated as electrons flow through the chain, not at one complex alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecules move from high to low concentration, so concentrating protons against their gradient requires energy input.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TCA cycle produces the reduced coenzymes that feed the ETC; it does not pump protons itself.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A pharmacologist explains that the inner mitochondrial membrane acts as a barrier that allows a proton gradient to be maintained. Which property of protons makes this barrier effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their binding to coenzyme Q keeps them in the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their charge makes them impermeable to the lipid bilayer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their consumption by complex IV prevents accumulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their lipid solubility traps them within the membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their small size allows rapid diffusion through the bilayer

explanation.summary: Protons are charged and therefore impermeable to the lipid bilayers of the mitochondria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like a concrete dam that is impenetrable to water, the barrier of lipids within the mitochondria is a barrier to protons. Because protons are charged, they are impermeable to the lipid bilayers, so the lake of protons in the intermembrane space can only flow through a defined route, the ATP synthase spillway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coenzyme Q shuttles electrons, not protons, between complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complex IV passes electrons to oxygen; proton consumption by complex IV is not the reason the membrane is a barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protons are charged and not lipid-soluble; the lipid-soluble molecules in the ETC are coenzyme Q and cytochrome c.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protons do not freely diffuse through the bilayer; if they did, no gradient could be maintained.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A biophysicist tracks the movement of protons that pass through ATP synthase during active oxidative phosphorylation. In which direction do these protons flow through the enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From the cytosol into the intermembrane space

choices.label: B
choices.text: From the intermembrane space into the cytosol

choices.label: C
choices.text: From the intermembrane space into the matrix

choices.label: D
choices.text: From the matrix into the cytosol

choices.label: E
choices.text: From the matrix into the intermembrane space

explanation.summary: Protons concentrated in the intermembrane space flow down their gradient through ATP synthase into the matrix.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ETC translocates protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a lake of protons there. These protons are allowed to flow from high concentration to lower concentration specifically through the ATP synthase spillway, returning to the matrix, and ATP synthase converts this electrochemical movement into ATP synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner membrane, so it does not move protons between the cytosol and the intermembrane space.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protons flow through ATP synthase across the inner membrane, not outward across the outer membrane into the cytosol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ATP synthase spans the inner membrane between the intermembrane space and matrix, not between the matrix and cytosol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Matrix-to-intermembrane-space movement is the direction protons are pumped by the ETC, against their gradient, not the direction of flow through ATP synthase.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: ATP synthase is sometimes referred to as complex V of the electron transport chain. Which of the following correctly distinguishes complex V from complexes I through IV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complex V accepts electrons directly from FADH2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complex V does not participate directly in electron transfer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complex V is embedded in the outer mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complex V passes electrons to oxygen as terminal acceptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complex V shuttles electrons to cytochrome c

explanation.summary: ATP synthase (complex V) is powered by the proton gradient but does not itself transfer electrons.
explanation.whyCorrect: ATP synthase is fully dependent on the flow of protons for the catalytic production of ATP and is sometimes called complex V of the ETC. Unlike complexes I through IV, however, it does not participate directly in electron transfer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FADH2 donates its electrons to complex II, not to ATP synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ATP synthase, like the ETC complexes, is embedded within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complex IV passes electrons to oxygen, the terminal acceptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complex III passes electrons to cytochrome c; ATP synthase handles protons, not electrons.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A biochemist lists the inputs and outputs of the electron transport chain during coupled oxidative phosphorylation. Which of the following is a substrate consumed by the ETC rather than a product it generates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP

choices.label: B
choices.text: H2O

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heat

choices.label: D
choices.text: NAD+

choices.label: E
choices.text: O2

explanation.summary: The ETC consumes O2, NADH, and FADH2 and produces ATP and H2O when coupled.
explanation.whyCorrect: The substrates of ETC/OXPHOS are O2, NADH, and FADH2. Electrons from the reduced coenzymes are transferred through the complexes and ultimately to oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor, generating H2O and, when coupled to ATP synthase, ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is the general product of coupled ETC/OXPHOS, not a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Water is produced when electrons are passed to oxygen; it is a product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heat is a product of uncoupled ETC, not a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAD+ is regenerated when NADH donates its electrons to complex I; it is the substrate NADH, not NAD+, that the ETC consumes.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a genetic disorder that compromises the ability of his mitochondria to sustain cellular energy needs, producing weakness in multiple organs. Which of the following best describes the relationship between where this inborn error originates and where it manifests?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Originates and manifests exclusively within the cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Originates at the organelle level and manifests at the tissue or organ level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Originates at the tissue level and manifests at the organelle level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Originates at the whole-organ level without a cellular correlate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Originates in the lysosome and manifests as accrual of cellular waste

explanation.summary: Because metabolism is compartmentalized, inborn errors of metabolism produce localized organelle-level defects that manifest at the tissue or organ level.
explanation.whyCorrect: Due to the compartmentalization of metabolic processes, an inborn error of metabolism often has a localized, specific cellular defect. While this primary defect results in many secondary deleterious effects, it originates at the organelle level and then manifests at the tissue or organ level. Mitochondrial diseases are a collection of disorders from varied genetic disruptions that compromise the ability of the mitochondria to sustain cellular energy needs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial diseases originate within the mitochondria, not the cytosol, and they manifest at the tissue or organ level.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The direction is reversed; the primary defect is in the organelle and its consequences appear in tissues and organs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inborn errors have a specific cellular and organelle-level origin; they are not defects that exist only at the organ level.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysosomal enzyme disruption with waste accrual describes lysosomal storage disease, not a mitochondrial disorder.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview II: OXPHOS
