explanation.summary: RBCs rely on glycolysis because they lack mitochondria, not because they lack oxygen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mature RBCs completely lack organelles, including mitochondria, so they cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation and must generate ATP by glycolysis with lactate production. This metabolic preference also spares the abundant oxygen they carry for delivery to the tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The biconcave shape enhances gas diffusion and flexibility; it is not the reason for glycolytic dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The RBC membrane is highly flexible, not thick and rigid, and membrane properties do not dictate the metabolic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RBCs actually carry high concentrations of oxygen bound to hemoglobin; oxygen supply is not the limiting factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mature RBCs lack a nucleus entirely, so a nucleus cannot be consuming ATP.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A first-year medical student examines a peripheral blood smear and notes that normal red blood cells display a pale region in their center under light microscopy. Which of the following best explains this central pallor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin is concentrated only at the cell periphery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitochondria localize to the middle of the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells are rigid spheres that lack organelles

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cells are thinner in the middle and thicker at the edges

choices.label: E
choices.text: The convex surface of the cell diffracts light

explanation.summary: Central pallor reflects the biconcave disc shape, which is thinner in the center.
explanation.whyCorrect: RBCs are biconcave discs whose thinner central region transmits more light during imaging, making it appear paler than the rest of the cell. Expansion or loss of this central pallor can be an important clinical observation in RBC disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin fills the cell; the pale center is due to reduced cell thickness there, not absence of hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mature RBCs lack mitochondria entirely, so they cannot localize to the center.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rigid spheres, as in hereditary spherocytosis, actually lack central pallor rather than displaying it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RBC surface is concave, not convex, and pallor is due to light transmission through the thin center, not diffraction.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has intermittent jaundice and splenomegaly, and his red blood cells appear as rigid spheres lacking central pallor. When his red cells are placed in progressively hypotonic solutions, they lyse more readily than control cells. Mutation in which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mitochondrial electron transport chain complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytoskeletal and membrane proteins of the RBC

choices.label: D
choices.text: The beta-globin chain of hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gamma-globin chain of hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis results from mutations in RBC cytoskeletal/membrane proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hereditary spherocytosis, mutations in cytoskeletal or membrane proteins produce rigid spheres that lack central pallor and are prone to lysis and splenic turnover. A positive osmotic fragility test, in which the patient's RBCs lyse more readily than controls in hypotonic solution, supports this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mature RBCs lack mitochondria, so an electron transport chain mutation cannot explain these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase makes 2,3-BPG and modulates oxygen affinity; it does not cause spherical, fragile cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A beta-globin substitution causes sickle cell disease, producing crescent-shaped cells rather than rigid spheres with a positive osmotic fragility test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The gamma chain is a component of fetal hemoglobin and is unrelated to membrane structure.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has episodes of severe extremity pain and fatigue. A blood smear shows crescent-shaped red blood cells. The underlying defect is a single amino acid substitution in hemoglobin. Which change best describes this substitution and its primary consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gamma chain replaced entirely by a beta chain, lowering hemoglobin oxygen affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: A nonpolar valine replaced by a polar glutamate, increasing hemoglobin solubility

choices.label: C
choices.text: A polar glutamate replaced by nonpolar valine, promoting hemoglobin polymerization

choices.label: D
choices.text: A polar histidine replaced by nonpolar valine, abolishing the Bohr effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the heme porphyrin ring from each globin, preventing oxygen binding

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease is caused by a glutamate-to-valine substitution that promotes Hb polymerization.
explanation.whyCorrect: In sickle cell disease, a polar, negatively charged glutamate is replaced by a nonpolar valine within the hemoglobin tetramer. This decreases solubility and promotes polymerization of hemoglobin, distorting the cell into a crescent shape, which is the primary cause of the disease pathology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sickle cell disease involves an amino acid substitution within a chain, not replacement of an entire gamma chain by a beta chain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The substitution goes the opposite direction (polar to nonpolar) and decreases, not increases, solubility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The substitution involves glutamate and valine, not histidine, and does not target the Bohr effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The heme porphyrin ring is intact; the defect lies in a globin amino acid substitution.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher compares the oxygen-binding curves of myoglobin and adult hemoglobin plotted together. In actively metabolizing peripheral muscle tissue, hemoglobin has released oxygen and is only about 50% saturated, while myoglobin saturation approaches 100% in the same environment. Which property of myoglobin best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Myoglobin circulates within red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Myoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myoglobin has a higher P50 than hemoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myoglobin is a tetramer that shows binding cooperativity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myoglobin releases oxygen more readily than hemoglobin at low pO2

explanation.summary: Myoglobin has the highest oxygen affinity, allowing it to take up oxygen in tissue where Hb unloads it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myoglobin has the greatest oxygen affinity of the oxygen-carrying proteins (P50 about 2.8 versus 26 for hemoglobin), so it binds oxygen where hemoglobin in RBCs is releasing it. This lets myoglobin remain nearly fully saturated in tissue even as hemoglobin drops toward 50% saturation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myoglobin is expressed in tissue such as muscle, whereas hemoglobin is the protein within circulating RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A higher P50 indicates lower affinity; myoglobin has a lower P50 (higher affinity) than hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myoglobin is a monomer and lacks cooperativity, giving it a hyperbolic rather than sigmoidal curve.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Because of its high affinity, myoglobin holds onto oxygen tightly rather than releasing it readily at low pO2.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A physiologist explains that during pregnancy, oxygen must be transferred from maternal blood to fetal blood across the placenta. Compared with adult hemoglobin (HbA), fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is best characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has a higher oxygen affinity than myoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has a higher oxygen affinity, with a curve shifted to the left of HbA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has a lower oxygen affinity, with a curve shifted to the right of HbA

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a monomer that lacks binding cooperativity

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is composed of two alpha and two beta chains

explanation.summary: HbF has a higher oxygen affinity than HbA, shifting its curve left to favor maternal-to-fetal transfer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fetal hemoglobin is tetrameric (two alpha and two gamma chains) and, like HbA, shows cooperativity, but its sigmoidal curve is shifted to the left of HbA, indicating higher oxygen affinity. This higher affinity allows oxygen exchange from the mother to the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HbF affinity is still lower than that of myoglobin, which has the highest affinity of the three.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbF has higher affinity than HbA, so its curve is shifted left, not right.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbF is tetrameric and does show cooperativity; myoglobin is the monomer that lacks cooperativity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbF is composed of two alpha and two gamma chains; two alpha and two beta chains describe HbA.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: During intense exercise, a skeletal muscle produces lactate because oxygen availability is limited relative to demand, creating a localized area of low pH. According to the Bohr effect, how does this low pH alter hemoglobin, and what is the benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts hemoglobin to carboxyhemoglobin, increasing oxygen delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: It decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve right and releasing more oxygen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no effect on hemoglobin affinity because pH acts only on myoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen by deprotonating histidine residues

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve left and retaining oxygen

explanation.summary: Low pH (Bohr effect) decreases Hb oxygen affinity, right-shifting the curve to release more O2 to active tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the Bohr effect, elevated H+ protonates histidine residues (pKa about 6.5) in hemoglobin, stabilizing a lower-affinity form that favors oxygen dissociation. This right shift promotes increased oxygen release to an active muscle that needs it to recover its metabolic demand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carboxyhemoglobin is formed by carbon monoxide, not by low pH, and it impairs rather than increases delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low pH acts on hemoglobin through the Bohr effect, altering its oxygen affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low pH protonates (not deprotonates) histidine residues, and the result is decreased affinity, not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low pH decreases affinity and shifts the curve right; it does not retain oxygen.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: At high altitude, tissue demand for oxygen rises and red blood cells increase production of a glucose-derived molecule that lowers hemoglobin affinity for oxygen. This molecule is generated from a glycolytic intermediate by an enzyme in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. Which molecule and precursor are correctly described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2,3-BPG, formed from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2,3-BPG, formed from glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbaminohemoglobin, formed from CO2 binding to globin chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbonic acid, formed from CO2 and water by carbonic anhydrase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lactate, formed from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase

explanation.summary: 2,3-BPG is made from 1,3-BPG by bisphosphoglycerate mutase and lowers Hb oxygen affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) is formed in RBCs from the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate by the enzyme bisphosphoglycerate mutase within the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. It lowers hemoglobin affinity for oxygen and can be produced rapidly in response to increased tissue demand or lower oxygen availability.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 2,3-BPG derives from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate via bisphosphoglycerate mutase, not from glucose-6-phosphate via hexokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbaminohemoglobin is formed by CO2 binding hemoglobin, not from a glycolytic intermediate by a mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbonic acid forms from CO2 and water and drives the Bohr effect but is not the glucose-derived 2,3-BPG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactate is made from pyruvate and lowers local pH, but it is not the 2,3-BPG molecule described here.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found in a garage with a running car engine. He has headache, dizziness, and altered mental status. His standard pulse oximetry reads normal. Which of the following best explains his condition and its initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhemoglobin; treat with high-flow 100% oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon monoxide lowers hemoglobin oxygen affinity; treat with a paper bag

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyanide inhibits the electron transport chain; treat with intravenous glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methemoglobin forms from oxidized iron; treat by lowering inspired oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; treat with rebreathing

explanation.summary: CO poisoning forms carboxyhemoglobin and is treated with high-flow 100% oxygen to displace CO.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbon monoxide binds the same heme site as oxygen with over 200 times the affinity, forming carboxyhemoglobin, which reduces oxygen carrying and increases affinity for the little O2 still bound, causing tissue hypoxia. Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish CO-bound from O2-bound hemoglobin, so it reads normal; treatment is continuous high-flow 100% oxygen to competitively displace the bound CO.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CO increases hemoglobin oxygen affinity (a left shift), and a paper bag is used for hyperventilation, not CO poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is carbon monoxide from car exhaust, not cyanide, and glucose is not the treatment; CO impairs delivery rather than blocking the electron transport chain like cyanide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The scenario describes CO exposure, not methemoglobinemia, and lowering inspired oxygen would worsen hypoxia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis does not fit a garage exposure with normal pulse oximetry and altered mental status.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical student develops tingling in the fingers, difficulty breathing, and dizziness while jogging under exam stress. A caregiver has her sit and breathe into a paper bag. Which of the following best explains the underlying disturbance and why the paper bag helps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hyperventilation causes respiratory acidosis; the bag removes excess CO2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperventilation forms carboxyhemoglobin; the bag displaces carbon monoxide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperventilation increases 2,3-BPG, shifting the curve right; the bag lowers 2,3-BPG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperventilation lowers CO2 and H+, increasing hemoglobin oxygen affinity; rebreathing restores CO2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hyperventilation raises CO2, decreasing hemoglobin oxygen affinity; the bag adds oxygen

explanation.summary: Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, left-shifting the Hb curve; rebreathing restores CO2 and delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged rapid expiration of CO2 during hyperventilation produces respiratory alkalosis and the loss of two allosteric regulators of Hb-O2 binding, CO2 and H+. Losing these regulators increases hemoglobin oxygen affinity (a left shift) and decreases delivery to peripheral tissues; breathing into a paper bag lets the patient re-inhale exhaled CO2, restoring CO2 levels and proper oxygen delivery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis, because CO2 is blown off rather than retained.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carboxyhemoglobin forms from carbon monoxide exposure, which is not occurring in this exercise-and-anxiety scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperventilation does not increase 2,3-BPG; the disturbance is loss of CO2 and H+ causing a left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperventilation lowers, not raises, CO2, and the resulting change increases affinity rather than decreasing it.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with several days of vomiting and poor fluid intake has a hematocrit of 52% (reference 41-50), while his total red cell mass is estimated to be normal. Which of the following best explains the elevated hematocrit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia from chronic blood loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dehydration reducing plasma volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of red cells to splenic turnover

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced hemoglobin concentration

explanation.summary: Hematocrit is the RBC fraction of blood volume, so losing plasma water artificially raises it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematocrit measures the percentage of whole blood volume occupied by RBCs. Decreasing the overall volume by reducing the solvent (water), as in dehydration from vomiting, artificially inflates the hematocrit even when the actual red cell mass is normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia is defined by a decrease in hematocrit (among other values), so it cannot explain a high hematocrit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An increased MCV indicates larger cells (macrocytic anemia) but does not increase the fraction of blood volume occupied by RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of red cells to splenic turnover would lower the red cell mass and hematocrit, not raise it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A reduced hemoglobin concentration accompanies anemia and low hematocrit, the opposite of the finding here.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old healthy man donates blood, and a sample is centrifuged so that the cellular components separate from the plasma. Red blood cells are the largest cellular component of blood. Approximately what fraction of whole blood volume do RBCs typically occupy in a healthy person?

explanation.summary: RBCs make up roughly 45% of blood by volume, a percentage reported clinically as the hematocrit.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red blood cells are the largest cellular component of blood, comprising about 45% of blood by volume. The percentage of whole blood derived from RBC content is the hematocrit (HCT), a critical CBC value.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5% is far below the normal RBC fraction; a value this low would represent profound anemia rather than a healthy sample.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 25% is well below the typical RBC fraction and would indicate a markedly reduced hematocrit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 65% exceeds the normal RBC fraction; RBCs do not occupy nearly two thirds of blood volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 85% is far above the normal RBC fraction; plasma occupies more than half of blood volume in health.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old electroplating worker is brought to the emergency department after an accidental exposure to a cyanide-containing solution. He is confused and hypotensive, yet his skin appears flushed and red. Which of the following best explains the red skin discoloration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocked electron transport leaves O2 unconsumed, keeping hemoglobin oxygenated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon monoxide binds heme and forms bright red carboxyhemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated CO2 forms carbaminohemoglobin, which is red when saturated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin polymerization traps oxygenated cells in dermal capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased 2,3-BPG production drives hemoglobin to release O2 in the skin

explanation.summary: Cyanide inhibits the ETC, so tissues cannot consume O2 and RBCs remain full of red oxygenated hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term red blood cell derives from the color of oxygenated hemoglobin. Because the ETC inhibitor cyanide blocks O2 consumption through OXPHOS, oxygen is not unloaded and used by tissues, increasing the amount of oxygenated Hb within RBCs and producing a red discoloration of the skin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This is a cyanide exposure, not carbon monoxide; carboxyhemoglobin is not involved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbaminohemoglobin forms from CO2 binding and has decreased O2 affinity; it does not account for the red color.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin polymerization occurs in sickle cell disease, which is unrelated to cyanide poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2,3-BPG lowers Hb affinity to release oxygen; it does not explain retained oxygenated Hb after cyanide exposure.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A hematology researcher calculates that the membrane surface area of a healthy red blood cell (about 140 um^2) substantially exceeds the surface area of a sphere that could simply enclose the same cell contents (about 98 um^2). Which of the following is the primary functional benefit of this excess membrane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows the cell to retain its nucleus during maturation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lets the cell deform while passing through narrow vascular beds

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides space for mitochondria to carry out oxidative phosphorylation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises the mean corpuscular volume above the reference range

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reduces the cell's dependence on glucose for ATP production

explanation.summary: The biconcave shape gives the RBC extra membrane that permits deformation and maximizes gas diffusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The biconcave disc bestows the RBC with more membrane than a simple sphere would have. This extra membrane and its supporting cytoskeleton allow the red cell to be stretched and deformed by mechanical stresses as it passes through narrow vascular beds, and they provide additional surface area to maximize gas diffusion for O2 and CO2 exchange.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mature RBCs lack nuclei entirely; membrane surface area has nothing to do with nuclear retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mature RBCs completely lack mitochondria and organelles; the extra membrane does not house them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MCV reflects average cell volume, not membrane surface area; a healthy RBC has a normal MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RBCs remain strictly reliant on glucose for glycolytic ATP regardless of membrane area.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease presents with severe pain in his hands and feet that began after a day of vigorous play. His hemoglobin carries a glutamate-to-valine substitution. Which of the following best explains his pain episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbaminohemoglobin accumulates in peripheral capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased osmotic fragility leads to intravascular lysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Misshapen cells obstruct small vascular spaces

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protonated histidine residues cause excess O2 unloading

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rigid spherical cells undergo rapid splenic turnover

explanation.summary: Sickled RBCs cannot transit small vascular spaces, producing painful vascular occlusions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low solubility of the mutant Hb tetramer causes polymerization and membrane distortion into a crescent shape. The misshapen RBCs cannot properly transit within or through small vascular spaces, causing painful and harmful vascular occlusions; they also carry O2 poorly, compromising OXPHOS and producing chronic fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbaminohemoglobin is a natural CO2-carrying form of Hb and does not cause vaso-occlusive pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A positive osmotic fragility test characterizes hereditary spherocytosis; sickle pain arises from occlusion, not osmotic lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histidine protonation is the Bohr effect, a normal physiologic modulator of affinity, not the cause of sickle pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rigid spheres susceptible to splenic turnover describe hereditary spherocytosis, not sickle cell disease.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A complete blood count from a 40-year-old woman includes the value 13.6 g/dL. Which of the following CBC parameters is reported in these units?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematocrit percentage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed cell volume percentage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell count

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin concentration is the concentration of Hb in whole blood, reported in grams per deciliter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the standard CBC values, hemoglobin concentration is defined as the concentration of Hb in whole blood expressed in grams/deciliter (g/dL). A value of 13.6 g/dL is therefore a hemoglobin concentration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematocrit is the percentage of total blood volume contributed by RBCs and is reported as a percent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MCV is the average volume of the RBCs, typically reported in femtoliters (fL).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed cell volume is another name for hematocrit and is reported as a percentage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RBC count is the number of RBCs per microliter of blood volume, not a mass concentration.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A laboratory report for a 55-year-old man lists a packed cell volume of 38%, and a medical student is unsure how to interpret this term. Which of the following does this value describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average volume of an individual circulating RBC

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concentration of hemoglobin within whole blood in g/dL

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of RBCs contained in a microliter of blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: The percentage of circulating hemoglobin that is saturated with oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The percentage of total blood volume contributed by RBCs

explanation.summary: Packed cell volume is another name for hematocrit, the RBC percentage of total blood volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematocrit is sometimes referred to as the packed cell volume because of the analytic method used to obtain it. It is defined as the percentage of total blood volume contributed by RBCs, so a packed cell volume of 38% means RBCs occupy 38% of whole blood volume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The average RBC volume is the mean corpuscular volume, reported in fL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin concentration is a separate CBC value reported in g/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The number of RBCs per microliter is the RBC count, not the packed cell volume.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percent Hb saturation is a point on the oxygen dissociation curve, not a CBC parameter.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman reports several weeks of fatigue, shortness of breath when climbing stairs, and muscle weakness. Examination shows pale nail beds and pale conjunctivae. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL (reference 11.9-14.8). Which of the following best accounts for her fatigue and weakness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated 2,3-BPG prevents hemoglobin from loading O2 in the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess lactate from RBC glycolysis acidifies skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of central pallor impairs gas diffusion across the RBC

choices.label: D
choices.text: RBC mitochondria consume the oxygen intended for muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced O2 delivery compromises OXPHOS and ATP production

explanation.summary: Anemia symptoms reflect insufficient O2 delivery, which limits OXPHOS and ATP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Much of the symptomatology of anemia is accounted for by a lack of O2 delivery to the tissues. Compromised OXPHOS prevents sufficient ATP production for biochemical needs, so fatigue, shortness of breath, and muscle weakness are common presentations, and the general lack of sufficient RBCs produces pallor in nail beds and mucosal membranes such as the lining of the eye.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG lowers affinity to aid unloading in tissues; it does not prevent loading in the lungs or explain anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RBC lactate production is normal metabolism and is not the cause of anemia symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Central pallor is a normal microscopic feature of RBCs; its loss describes spherocytes, not this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature RBCs lack mitochondria and do not consume the oxygen they carry.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a routine CBC: hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (reference 13.5-17.5), hematocrit 34% (reference 41-50), and MCV 72 fL (reference 80-96). He reports no fatigue, dyspnea, or weakness, and there is no pallor on examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia is excluded because he has no symptoms or pallor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microcytic anemia is present and its underlying cause must be sought

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings should be classified as normocytic given the normal exam

choices.label: D
choices.text: The low MCV establishes the final diagnosis without further testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: The values reflect dehydration rather than a reduced RBC mass

explanation.summary: Anemia is defined by the CBC values, MCV classifies it, and the classification is only the start of finding the cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia is clinically defined by a reduction in RBC count, Hb concentration, or hematocrit, and here both Hb and HCT are low. An MCV below the reference range classifies it as microcytic. Such classifications are not the end diagnosis but aid in identifying the underlying cause, which is of paramount importance; in practice a person can have a low HCT without symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia is defined by the laboratory values, and the brick stresses that a person can have a low HCT without symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Classification depends on the MCV, which is below the reference range, so the anemia is microcytic regardless of the exam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MCV classification is explicitly not to be considered the end diagnosis; the underlying basis must still be identified.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dehydration artificially raises hematocrit by reducing plasma water; it does not produce a low hematocrit.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman who is not pregnant has the composition of her hemoglobin analyzed. Which of the following best describes the expected result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Almost entirely two alpha and two gamma chains

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbA only, with fetal hemoglobin completely absent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mostly monomeric globin lacking cooperativity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mostly two alpha and two beta chains, with 1-2% HbF

choices.label: E
choices.text: Roughly equal amounts of HbA and HbF

explanation.summary: Adult hemoglobin is mostly HbA (alpha2 beta2) with a small 1-2% fraction of HbF (alpha2 gamma2).
explanation.whyCorrect: Most hemoglobin in adults is in the form of HbA, composed of two alpha chains and two beta chains, with a small amount (1%-2%) composed of HbF, which contains two alpha chains and two gamma chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two alpha and two gamma chains describe HbF, which is only a minor component in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A small amount of HbF (1-2%) persists in adults; it is not completely absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin is a tetramer with cooperativity; monomeric globin describes myoglobin, which is expressed in tissue, not blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbF is only 1-2% of adult hemoglobin, not an equal share with HbA.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A physiologist notes that fetal hemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than HbA yet a lower affinity than myoglobin. Which of the following best explains why HbF affinity does not exceed that of myoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HbF contains beta chains that lower its affinity toward that of HbA

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbF exists in multiple distinct forms, unlike myoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbF is a monomer that lacks oxygen-binding cooperativity

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbF is expressed in fetal tissue rather than in erythrocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbF must still unload oxygen to myoglobin-containing fetal tissues

explanation.summary: HbF affinity is intermediate: high enough to take O2 from maternal HbA, but low enough to deliver it to fetal Mb.
explanation.whyCorrect: Affinities are distinct among the oxygen-carrying proteins so that some can drop off oxygen where others pick it up. HbF has the next highest affinity after Mb to allow exchange from mother to fetus, but its affinity is still lower than Mb because HbF must deliver oxygen to fetal tissues, which contain Mb.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HbF contains two alpha and two gamma chains, not beta chains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is Hb that has distinct forms (HbA, HbF); there are not distinct forms of Mb, and this does not explain the affinity ordering.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbF is tetrameric like HbA and exhibits cooperativity with a sigmoidal curve; myoglobin is the monomer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbA and HbF are both expressed within circulating erythrocytes; Mb is the protein expressed in tissue.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemist observes that once one oxygen molecule binds to a hemoglobin tetramer, subtle structural changes make binding of the next oxygen to another subunit more favorable, and release of one oxygen favors release of another. Which of the following is the principal physiologic advantage of this property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hyperbolic dissociation curve identical to that of myoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: An oxygen affinity that exceeds that of myoglobin in muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Constant saturation regardless of the partial pressure of oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid O2 loading in the lungs and rapid unloading in depleted tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance to competitive binding by carbon monoxide

explanation.summary: Cooperativity tailors Hb binding to location: fast loading in the O2-rich lungs and fast unloading in the periphery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Binding cooperativity among the globin subunits produces the sigmoidal curve and allows rapid binding of oxygen within the oxygen-rich environment of the lungs as well as rapid unloading in depleted areas. Cooperativity is how Hb maximizes its oxygen binding so that it is tailored to select bodily locales, the lungs for loading and peripheral tissues for unloading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cooperativity produces a sigmoidal curve; the hyperbolic curve belongs to monomeric myoglobin, which lacks cooperativity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Under normal physiologic conditions HbA has the lowest affinity of the three proteins; Mb has the greatest.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cooperativity makes saturation change steeply with pO2, which is the opposite of constant saturation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CO binds the same heme site with more than 200 times the affinity of O2; cooperativity does not prevent this.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: An experimental compound lowers the P50 of adult hemoglobin from 26 mm Hg to 18 mm Hg without changing the sigmoidal shape of its dissociation curve. Which of the following best describes the effect of this compound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased O2 affinity with a leftward shift, increasing tissue delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased O2 affinity with a rightward shift, increasing tissue delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased O2 affinity with a leftward shift, reducing tissue delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased O2 affinity with a rightward shift, reducing tissue delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged O2 affinity, because P50 reflects only the lung environment

explanation.summary: A lower P50 means 50% saturation is reached at a lower pO2, i.e., higher affinity and a left-shifted curve.
explanation.whyCorrect: P50 is the partial pressure of oxygen at which the protein is 50% saturated. Myoglobin's P50 of about 2.8 versus hemoglobin's 26 illustrates that a lower P50 reflects higher affinity. Lowering HbA's P50 therefore shifts the curve to the left, increasing affinity and delaying dissociation in the periphery, which decreases delivery to tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A leftward shift indicates increased, not decreased, affinity, and it reduces rather than increases tissue delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A rightward shift corresponds to a higher P50 and decreased affinity, the opposite of a fall in P50.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased affinity is correct, but it corresponds to a leftward shift, not a rightward one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P50 directly reports affinity across the whole curve; a change from 26 to 18 mm Hg is a real change in affinity.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: In peripheral capillaries, a portion of the CO2 produced by tissue metabolism binds directly to hemoglobin, forming a naturally modified species. Which of the following correctly identifies this species and its properties?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbaminohemoglobin, which carries about 10-20% of CO2 and has decreased O2 affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbaminohemoglobin, which carries most CO2 and has increased O2 affinity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbonic acid bound to heme, which carries about 10-20% of CO2 and raises O2 affinity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carboxyhemoglobin, which carries about 10-20% of CO2 and has decreased O2 affinity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Carboxyhemoglobin, which carries most CO2 and has increased O2 affinity

explanation.summary: Carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2) carries roughly 10-20% of CO2 and has reduced affinity for O2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enriching CO2 augments the formation of carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2), a natural modification of Hb by CO2 that accounts for about 10-20% of CO2 transport. This form of Hb has a decreased affinity for oxygen binding, which is the second of the two ways elevated pCO2 lowers Hb affinity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbaminohemoglobin carries only about 10-20% of CO2, and it has decreased, not increased, O2 affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbonic acid forms in the bicarbonate buffer from CO2 and water; it does not bind heme, and it lowers rather than raises affinity via H+.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carboxyhemoglobin is a CO adduct with increased affinity for the O2 that remains bound; it plays no role in CO2 transport.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) is formed by carbon monoxide, not CO2, and it is not a CO2 transport species.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: During strenuous exercise, CO2 accumulates in the capillaries supplying active muscle. Apart from direct binding to hemoglobin, elevated pCO2 lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity through the blood buffer system. Which of the following sequences best describes this pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CO2 binds heme iron directly, displacing O2 from the porphyrin ring

choices.label: B
choices.text: CO2 forms carbonic acid with water, raising [H+] that protonates histidine

choices.label: C
choices.text: CO2 lowers local temperature, reducing kinetic energy for dissociation

choices.label: D
choices.text: CO2 raises plasma pH, deprotonating histidine residues in hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: CO2 stimulates bisphosphoglycerate mutase, raising 2,3-BPG production

explanation.summary: Elevated CO2 shifts the bicarbonate buffer toward carbonic acid, raising [H+] and producing the Bohr effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated CO2 causes a shift in the bicarbonate blood buffer wherein CO2 combines with water to produce more carbonic acid (H2CO3). The increased concentration of this weak acid pushes the equilibrium toward increased [H+], which protonates histidine residues (pKa about 6.5) in Hb and stabilizes the lower-affinity form, the Bohr effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CO2 does not bind the heme iron; the direct Hb modification by CO2 is carbaminohemoglobin formation on the protein, and this stem asks about the buffer pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CO2 does not lower temperature; active muscle raises temperature, which increases rather than reduces dissociation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CO2 lowers pH rather than raising it, and it is protonation, not deprotonation, of histidine that reduces affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2,3-BPG is made from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt in response to tissue oxygen demand, not as a CO2 buffer response.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman runs a marathon on a warm day, and the temperature within her actively contracting leg muscles rises above core body temperature. Which of the following best describes the effect of this local temperature increase on hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of HbA to HbF to raise oxygen uptake

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of carboxyhemoglobin within muscle capillaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased kinetic energy, promoting rapid O2 dissociation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased O2 affinity, delaying dissociation in the periphery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of cooperativity, producing a hyperbolic curve

explanation.summary: High temperature lowers Hb affinity by adding kinetic energy that favors O2 dissociation to active muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: High temperature is one of the factors that decreases Hb affinity for O2. It increases the kinetic energy allowing for rapid dissociation, and this response is meant to aid a physically active muscle by enhancing oxygen delivery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HbA and HbF are distinct proteins with different chains; one does not convert to the other with temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carboxyhemoglobin forms only with carbon monoxide exposure, not with exercise-related warming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher temperature decreases affinity and speeds dissociation; increased affinity would result from lower temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Temperature shifts the sigmoidal curve but does not abolish cooperativity of the tetramer.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is found outdoors after a night of freezing temperatures; his core body temperature is 32 C (89.6 F). Which of the following changes in hemoglobin oxygen binding is expected in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of the Bohr effect through histidine protonation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased 2,3-BPG synthesis that lowers affinity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leftward shift of the curve with reduced O2 release to tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change, because temperature affects only myoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rightward shift of the curve with enhanced O2 release to tissues

explanation.summary: Low temperature raises Hb affinity (left shift) by decreasing kinetic energy, reducing O2 release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taking the list of factors that decrease affinity and reversing the change produces the opposite effect: low temperature decreases kinetic energy, reducing oxygen release, and shifts the curve to the left. Increased affinity delays dissociation in the periphery and decreases delivery to tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Bohr effect is driven by low pH (elevated H+), which is not the parameter altered here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2,3-BPG rises in response to increased tissue demand or lower oxygen abundance, not in response to cold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Temperature is a listed modulator of Hb affinity; the brick does not describe temperature acting on myoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rightward shift with enhanced release is the effect of high temperature, not hypothermia.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A physiologist wants to design in vitro conditions that maximally increase hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting its dissociation curve as far to the left as possible. Which of the following combinations would achieve this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased pH, decreased pCO2, increased temperature, decreased 2,3-BPG

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased pH, increased pCO2, decreased temperature, decreased 2,3-BPG

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased pH, increased pCO2, increased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased pH, decreased pCO2, decreased temperature, decreased 2,3-BPG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased pH, increased pCO2, decreased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG

explanation.summary: Reversing every right-shift factor (low pH, high pCO2, high temperature, high 2,3-BPG) gives a maximal left shift.
explanation.whyCorrect: The factors that decrease Hb affinity are low pH, elevated pCO2, high temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG, each shifting the curve to the right. Simply altering each change to its opposite (increased pH, decreased pCO2, decreased temperature, decreased 2,3-BPG) has the opposite effect on Hb-oxygen binding and shifts the curve to the left.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased pH and increased temperature both decrease affinity, working against the left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased pH and increased pCO2 both decrease affinity through the Bohr effect and carbaminohemoglobin formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is the complete set of right-shift factors and would minimize, not maximize, affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased pCO2 and increased 2,3-BPG both decrease affinity, working against the left shift.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old mountaineer acclimatizing at high altitude has markedly elevated 2,3-BPG in her red blood cells. Under these conditions, which of the following oxygen-binding proteins would exhibit the lowest oxygen affinity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HbA in a red blood cell with elevated 2,3-BPG

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbA in a red blood cell with normal 2,3-BPG

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbF in a red blood cell with normal 2,3-BPG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myoglobin in skeletal muscle exposed to elevated 2,3-BPG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myoglobin in skeletal muscle with normal 2,3-BPG

explanation.summary: HbA already has the lowest baseline affinity, and elevated 2,3-BPG lowers it further; Mb is unaffected by 2,3-BPG.
explanation.whyCorrect: HbA has the lowest general affinity for oxygen of the carrying proteins, and 2,3-BPG lowers HbA affinity further, so HbA in the presence of elevated 2,3-BPG has the lowest affinity of the options. Myoglobin has the highest affinity and its affinity is not altered by 2,3-BPG; HbF is next highest to allow exchange between mother and fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HbA with normal 2,3-BPG has lower affinity than Mb or HbF, but elevated 2,3-BPG lowers HbA affinity further still.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbF has a higher affinity than HbA (curve shifted left), so it cannot have the lowest affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myoglobin has the highest affinity of the proteins, and its affinity is not altered by 2,3-BPG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myoglobin has the greatest affinity regardless of 2,3-BPG level.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Four members of a family develop headache, dizziness, nausea, and fatigue over a winter evening while a gas-fueled space heater runs in a closed room; none of them noticed any unusual smell. Which of the following best describes the responsible agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon dioxide from complete combustion, recognized by its sharp odor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion, which is colorless and odorless

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyanide gas from the heater, which inhibits the electron transport chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Depletion of room oxygen by the flame, which lowers inspired pO2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lactate vapor from the fuel, which lowers blood pH

explanation.summary: CO is a tasteless, colorless, odorless gas released during incomplete combustion from stoves, heaters, and engines.
explanation.whyCorrect: CO is a tasteless, colorless, odorless gas released during incomplete combustion, unlike the CO2, H2O, and energy of complete combustion. It is generated from common sources such as car exhaust, structural fires, and gas-fueled stoves, heaters, and generators, and it produces dizziness, fatigue, nausea, and altered mental status through tissue hypoxia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete combustion yields CO2, H2O, and energy; CO2 is not the toxic product described, and the lack of odor points to CO.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyanide is an ETC inhibitor from other exposures; a gas heater produces CO through incomplete combustion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes heater-related poisoning to CO from incomplete combustion, not to oxygen depletion of the room.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactate is a metabolic product of glycolysis in cells, not a combustion gas.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with carbon monoxide poisoning has profound muscle weakness in addition to altered mental status. Beyond hemoglobin, which of the following proteins is directly impaired by CO, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase, because CO blocks the Rapoport-Luebering shunt

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbonic anhydrase, because CO competes with CO2 at its active site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactate dehydrogenase, because CO oxidizes its active site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myoglobin, because CO binds its heme prosthetic group

choices.label: E
choices.text: RBC cytoskeletal proteins, because CO rigidifies the membrane

explanation.summary: CO binds heme, so it impairs myoglobin in tissue as well as hemoglobin in RBCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: CO forms carboxyhemoglobin by binding the exact same Hb site as O2, and this binding occurs through the heme prosthetic group. Because myoglobin also carries a heme group, CO adversely impacts myoglobin function too, compounding the oxygen delivery decrement in tissues such as muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase makes 2,3-BPG from 1,3-BPG; it is not a heme protein and is not described as a CO target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbonic anhydrase participates in the bicarbonate buffer; CO toxicity is mediated through heme binding, not this enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate and is not a heme-containing target of CO.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytoskeletal and membrane protein defects characterize hereditary spherocytosis, not CO poisoning.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Two patients arrive at the emergency department: one after prolonged exposure to a running car engine in a closed garage, the other after ingesting a cyanide salt. Both are dizzy with altered mental status, and both have normal standard pulse oximetry readings. Which of the following best distinguishes cyanide toxicity from carbon monoxide toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cyanide forms carboxyhemoglobin, whereas CO inhibits the electron transport chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyanide impairs oxygen delivery, whereas CO impairs oxygen use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyanide lowers pulse oximetry readings, whereas CO does not

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cyanide produces a milder lactic acidosis than CO

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cyanide produces excitatory symptoms and impairs oxygen use rather than delivery

explanation.summary: CO impairs O2 delivery and CN impairs O2 use; symptoms overlap except for cyanide's excitatory features.
explanation.whyCorrect: With the exception of cyanide's excitatory symptoms, symptoms of CO toxicity are similar to those of cyanide because they systemically impair either oxygen delivery (CO) or oxygen use (CN). Standard pulse oximetry is unaffected by either agent, and CO can cause a lactic acidosis but typically not to the same extent as CN.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the mechanisms: CO forms carboxyhemoglobin, and cyanide inhibits the ETC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the mechanisms: CO impairs oxygen delivery, whereas cyanide impairs oxygen use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Standard pulse oximetry is unaffected by either agent, so it does not distinguish the two.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CO causes a lactic acidosis but typically not to the same extent as cyanide, so cyanide's acidosis is the more severe.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is rescued from a house fire. She is drowsy with blurred vision and nausea. Standard pulse oximetry reads 97%. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CO-oximetry to measure carboxyhemoglobin level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume on a complete blood count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test in hypotonic solution

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat standard pulse oximetry on another finger

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentration

explanation.summary: Carboxyhemoglobin is specifically measured by arterial blood gases or CO-oximetry, not by standard pulse oximetry.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structural fires are a common CO source, and blurred vision, nausea, and altered mental status are CO poisoning symptoms. Standard pulse oximetry does not differentiate hemoglobin bound to O2 from hemoglobin bound to CO, so it reads normal; carboxyhemoglobin and oxyhemoglobin levels can be specifically measured by arterial blood gases or by CO-oximetry available at many Emergency Departments.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MCV classifies anemia by cell size and provides no information about carboxyhemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic fragility testing diagnoses hereditary spherocytosis, not CO poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from oxyhemoglobin at any site, so repeating it is uninformative.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2,3-BPG is a natural affinity modulator and is not a diagnostic marker of CO exposure.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with confirmed carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with continuous high-flow oxygen (100% FiO2) by nonrebreather facemask over several hours. Which of the following best explains the rationale for this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High O2 competitively displaces CO bound to hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxygen converts carboxyhemoglobin into carbaminohemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxygen lowers blood pH, triggering the Bohr effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen oxidizes bound CO to CO2, which is then exhaled

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxygen raises 2,3-BPG, shifting the curve to the right

explanation.summary: Because CO and O2 compete for the same heme site, raising FiO2 from 21% to 100% displaces CO over hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: CO binds the same Hb site as O2, and competitive binding occurs because of structural similarity even though CO has more than 200 times the affinity. Since the CO became bound at room-air O2 levels (21% FiO2), immediate treatment involves continuous administration of high-flow supplemental oxygen (100% FiO2) by nonrebreather facemask or mechanical ventilation to competitively displace bound CO over several hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbaminohemoglobin is a CO2 adduct of Hb; COHb is not converted into it by oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxygen therapy does not act by lowering pH; the goal is to displace CO from heme, not to invoke the Bohr effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The therapy works by competition at the heme binding site, not by chemically oxidizing CO to CO2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2,3-BPG production responds to tissue demand and low oxygen abundance, and it is not the mechanism of oxygen therapy.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty gas generator has laboratory studies showing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbonic acid accumulates because CO blocks carbonic anhydrase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carboxyhemoglobin releases H+ as it forms in red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: CO directly protonates histidine residues in hemoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased 2,3-BPG synthesis consumes plasma bicarbonate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue hypoxia from impaired O2 delivery drives lactate production

explanation.summary: CO-induced tissue hypoxia forces lactate production, causing a high anion gap (lactic) metabolic acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of reduced O2 transport on RBCs and limited oxygen release from RBCs (because COHb has high affinity for the little O2 still bound) causes tissue hypoxia. Hypoxic tissue cannot sustain OXPHOS and produces lactate, so CO can cause a lactic acidosis, listed among CO poisoning findings as a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CO acts through heme binding; carbonic anhydrase inhibition is not part of its toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: COHb formation is competitive binding at the heme site and is not described as an acid-releasing reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histidine protonation is caused by elevated H+ (the Bohr effect), not by CO itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 2,3-BPG synthesis in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt does not consume bicarbonate or produce an anion gap acidosis.

questions.topicName: Metabolic Overview III: O2 Delivery (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue. Complete blood count shows anemia with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) above the reference range, and the peripheral smear shows abnormally large red blood cells. Which of the following best explains the increased cell size?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deficient porphyrin synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess membrane lipid deposition in the red cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased red cell turnover with otherwise normal morphology

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ineffective DNA synthesis with continued cytoplasmic growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insufficient globin chain production

explanation.summary: Macrocytic anemia arises when DNA synthesis is impaired but cytoplasmic growth continues, producing abnormally large red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In macrocytic anemia, cell division slows because of insufficient DNA synthesis while cytoplasmic development proceeds at a normal rate. The mismatch between growth and division yields abnormally large RBCs, and this defect also affects other rapidly dividing cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deficient porphyrin (heme) synthesis also causes microcytic, not macrocytic, anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Membrane lipid deposition is not the mechanism of macrocytosis described in nutritional anemias.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heightened red cell loss with normal morphology describes normocytic anemia, which has a normal MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insufficient globin drives microcytic anemia, producing small cells with a low MCV.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A patient from a severely impoverished region presents with cheilosis, glossitis, and a mild anemia with a normal MCV. An enzymatic assay of erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, measured before and after adding the relevant cofactor, yields an activity ratio of 1.4. Which of the following deficiencies is most consistent with these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine (B1)

explanation.summary: An erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity ratio above 1.2 indicates ariboflavinosis (vitamin B2 deficiency), the classically tested cause of normocytic nutritional anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Riboflavin is carried in flavoproteins as FMN/FAD, so a functional assay of erythrocyte glutathione reductase (a flavoprotein) reflects riboflavin status better than urine levels. A ratio above 1.2 signals deficiency. Because B2 is needed for maximal iron absorption and mild iron deficiency is normocytic, ariboflavinosis presents as normocytic anemia unless extremely severe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and would not be detected by this riboflavin-specific assay.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia, not a normal-MCV anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia and is not assessed by the glutathione reductase activity ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine deficiency is excluded from the anemia differential and does not cause the described picture.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man being treated for tuberculosis with a regimen that includes isoniazid develops a microcytic anemia along with a sensory neuropathy. Deficiency of a coenzyme for which of the following reactions best explains his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in mitochondria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduction of folate to tetrahydrofolate by dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first (committed) step of porphyrin (heme) synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfer of one-carbon units for thymidine synthesis

explanation.summary: Isoniazid causes vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency; pyridoxal 5'-phosphate is the coenzyme for the initial step of porphyrin synthesis, so deficiency yields microcytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the active B6 derivative, is required for the first step of porphyrin synthesis. Without adequate porphyrin, hemoglobin production falls and microcytic anemia results. Isoniazid is well known to impair B6, and the associated neuropathy fits the presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homocysteine to methionine is a B12/folate reaction associated with macrocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is a B12-dependent reaction, unrelated to microcytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduction of folate to FH4 is performed by DHFR and is a folate/macrocytic pathway, not the B6 microcytic mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: One-carbon transfer for thymidine is a folate function tied to macrocytic anemia.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with acute leukemia is treated with methotrexate, a structural analogue of folate. This antifolate impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells by directly inhibiting which of the following enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutathione reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methionine synthase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymidylate synthase

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is an antifolate that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking formation of the active one-carbon carrier tetrahydrofolate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate must undergo reductions catalyzed by DHFR to form tetrahydrofolate (FH4), the form used in one-carbon transfers. Methotrexate mimics folate and inhibits DHFR, restricting substrates needed for DNA synthesis. This is the milestone antifolate mechanism attributed to Sidney Farber's leukemia work.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione reductase is a riboflavin-linked flavoprotein, not the methotrexate target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methionine synthase uses methyl-B12 to convert homocysteine to methionine; it is not methotrexate's target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a B12-dependent enzyme unrelated to antifolate action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymidylate synthase is downstream and is not the enzyme methotrexate directly inhibits.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has macrocytic anemia, and laboratory testing is positive for anti-intrinsic factor antibodies. Impaired absorption of which vitamin, at which anatomical site, best accounts for her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin, absorbed in the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cobalamin, absorbed in the terminal ileum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate, absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate, absorbed in the terminal ileum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron, absorbed in the terminal ileum

explanation.summary: Intrinsic factor escorts cobalamin to the terminal ileum for absorption; antibodies against IF cause pernicious anemia and B12 malabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which facilitates cobalamin transit through the small intestine so it can be absorbed in the terminal ileum. Autoantibodies against IF (pernicious anemia) block this, producing macrocytic anemia. Presence of anti-IF antibodies is usually sufficient for the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin is absorbed in the terminal ileum, not the duodenum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate is absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum, but its uptake does not depend on intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate is not absorbed in the terminal ileum and is IF-independent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron absorption does not depend on intrinsic factor and does not cause macrocytic anemia.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with an undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency is treated with folate supplementation alone. His anemia partially improves, but over the following weeks his gait disturbance and paresthesias worsen. Which of the following best explains the danger of this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate corrects the anemia but does not prevent nerve damage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate directly binds and inactivates cobalamin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate inhibits DHFR and blocks its own activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate supplementation causes secondary iron overload

choices.label: E
choices.text: Folate worsens the anemia by trapping additional homocysteine

explanation.summary: Folate therapy can mask an underlying B12 deficiency: the anemia improves while progressive, irreversible neurologic damage continues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exogenous folate bypasses the methyl trap and restores FH4 intermediates for nucleic acid synthesis, so anemia symptoms improve temporarily. However, unlike folate deficiency, untreated B12 deficiency produces irreparable nerve damage. Thus folate can mask B12 deficiency while neurologic decline continues.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate does not physically bind or inactivate cobalamin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate does not inhibit DHFR; that is the action of the antifolate methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate does not cause iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate actually relieves the anemia transiently; it does not worsen it by trapping homocysteine.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: Two patients each present with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and elevated serum homocysteine. Only one of them also has an elevated methylmalonic acid (MMA) level. The elevated MMA most specifically indicates a deficiency of which vitamin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine (B1)

explanation.summary: Elevated MMA is unique to cobalamin (B12) deficiency and distinguishes it from folate deficiency, which shares elevated homocysteine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both folate and B12 deficiency elevate homocysteine and produce macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. However, MMA accumulates only when the B12-dependent conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA fails, so elevated MMA is specific for B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency elevates homocysteine but leaves MMA normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia and does not elevate MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency causes normocytic anemia and does not elevate MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine deficiency is not a cause of these hematologic or biochemical findings.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A patient with suspected nutritional anemia has an elevated urinary formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), a product of histidine catabolism. This older but still board-relevant biomarker most classically indicates a deficiency of which vitamin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Niacin (B3)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

explanation.summary: Elevated urinary FIGLU is a classic marker of folate deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: FIGLU is an intermediate of histidine catabolism whose further metabolism requires tetrahydrofolate. When folate is deficient, FIGLU accumulates and spills into the urine, making it a traditional (still board-tested) marker of folate deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B12 deficiency is more specifically indicated by elevated MMA, not by FIGLU.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Niacin deficiency is excluded from the anemia differential and is not marked by FIGLU.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxine deficiency is not marked by FIGLU.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Riboflavin status is assessed by the glutathione reductase activity ratio, not FIGLU.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents with new paresthesias and a macrocytic anemia. On questioning, the patient admits to recurrent recreational inhalation of nitrous oxide ('laughing gas'). Which of the following best explains the vitamin abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nitrous oxide accelerates renal excretion of folate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nitrous oxide binds the cobalt ion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrous oxide blocks iron absorption in the duodenum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nitrous oxide destroys gastric parietal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nitrous oxide inhibits dihydrofolate reductase

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by binding its cobalt ion, depleting functional B12 from both diet and stores.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12's structure contains a defining cobalt ion. N2O binds this cobalt, rendering the vitamin inert, and this rapidly inactivates all cobalamin whether obtained from diet or released from hepatic stores. This trend is increasingly seen in clinics and produces B12-deficiency findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: N2O does not act by increasing renal folate loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N2O does not impair duodenal iron absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N2O does not destroy parietal cells; that mechanism describes pernicious anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: N2O does not inhibit DHFR; that describes the antifolate methotrexate.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: While constructing a differential for a nutritional (B-vitamin) anemia, a student lists several B vitamins. A deficiency of which of the following would NOT be expected to cause anemia and should therefore be excluded from the differential?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine (B1)

explanation.summary: Thiamine (B1) is among the B vitamins excluded from the anemia differential; B2, B6, B9, and B12 all cause nutritional anemias.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists vitamins B1 (thiamine), B3 (niacin), B5 (pantothenate), and B7 (biotin) as vitamins that should be excluded when considering anemia. In contrast, riboflavin, pyridoxine, folate, and cobalamin each produce a nutritional anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and belongs in the differential.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and belongs in the differential.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia and belongs in the differential.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency causes normocytic anemia and belongs in the differential.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with a 4-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with fatigue, distended tender abdomen, and elevated liver enzymes. Laboratory studies show a macrocytic anemia. Given chronic alcohol use, which vitamin deficiency typically develops earliest and is the most likely initial contributor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine (B1)

explanation.summary: In chronic alcohol use, folate deficiency usually develops earlier than B12 deficiency because of folate's small body stores and direct alcohol-mediated malabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alcohol denatures GI proteins and damages the gut lining, and it directly impairs folate absorption and storage. Because folate stores are small (weeks to months), folate deficiency appears earlier, whereas B12 deficiency generally appears later after prolonged gastric or hepatic dysfunction. Accompanying malnutrition compounds the problem.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin deficiency generally appears later, since hepatic B12 stores last years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia, not the earliest macrocytic change here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency causes normocytic anemia and is not the classic earliest alcohol-related deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although thiamine is depleted in alcoholism, it is excluded from the anemia differential and does not explain the macrocytic anemia.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with pernicious anemia due to intrinsic factor antibodies undergoes laboratory evaluation. Compared with reference ranges, which of the following values is most likely to be elevated (above normal) in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematocrit (HCT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum iron

explanation.summary: Pernicious anemia is a macrocytic anemia, so MCV is elevated while the measures of red cell mass are low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cobalamin deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, producing abnormally large red cells and raising the MCV above normal. Because the patient is anemic, the hematocrit, hemoglobin, and red cell count are normal or, more likely, decreased rather than elevated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematocrit is reduced in anemia, not elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin concentration is low in an anemic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The red blood cell count is decreased in this anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum iron is not characteristically elevated by B12 deficiency and is unrelated to the macrocytosis.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy from a region with limited access to food is found to have anemia with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) below the reference range, and the peripheral smear shows abnormally small red blood cells. Which of the following best explains the reduced red cell size?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells sub-divide to reduce volume in pursuit of the needed Hb per cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytoplasmic volume continues to grow while nuclear division stalls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess DNA synthesis drives cell division faster than cell growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Functional cells are physically lost through bleeding or turnover

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased iron loading raises the Hb content of each cell
