explanation.summary: Microcytes form because RBCs have an inherent 'quota' of Hb per cell and sub-divide to shrink their volume when Hb is insufficient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microcytic anemia arises when insufficient globin protein or porphyrin is available for hemoglobin. Because RBC morphology is optimized to maximize Hb content, cells lacking sufficient Hb sub-divide to reduce overall cellular volume in a futile attempt to reach the needed Hb concentration per cell, producing microcytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Continued cytoplasmic growth with slowed division produces abnormally large cells (macrocytic anemia), not small ones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microcytosis stems from a lack of Hb, not from excess DNA synthesis; DNA synthesis defects produce macrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physical loss of otherwise normal cells describes normocytic anemia, in which morphology and MCV are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased Hb content per cell would not shrink the cell; microcytes reflect a deficit of Hb.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a chronically bleeding gastric ulcer is found to be anemic. His MCV is within the reference range, and red cell morphology on the peripheral smear is normal. Which of the following best characterizes his red blood cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells lacking porphyrin because the initial committed step of its synthesis failed in the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells produced by marrow progenitors whose DNA synthesis is compromised

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cells that grew in size but failed to divide and are not fully functional

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cells that reduced their volume because sufficient Hb could not be formed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Functional cells that are not present in the numbers needed because of physical loss

explanation.summary: Normocytic anemia reflects heightened red cell loss: the cells themselves are functional and normal in morphology, but too few are present.
explanation.whyCorrect: In normocytic anemia the MCV is within the reference range and morphology is normal. The anemia stems from a general loss of cells, which can derive from increased RBC turnover or bleeding, as in this patient with a bleeding ulcer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of the initial step of porphyrin synthesis (pyridoxine deficiency) yields microcytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Compromised DNA synthesis in progenitors is the defect underlying macrocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells that grow but fail to divide are macrocytes, associated with a high MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Volume reduction due to insufficient Hb describes microcytic anemia, which has a low MCV.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman takes several times the recommended daily amount of a B-complex supplement and asks whether she is at risk of vitamin toxicity. Which of the following statements best describes her risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All B vitamins are stored long term in the liver, so overload is common

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess B vitamins accumulate in fat, as vitamins A, D, E, and K do

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess B vitamins bind the cobalt ion and inactivate cobalamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess folate in the supplement inhibits dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypervitaminosis is rare because excess water-soluble vitamins are excreted

explanation.summary: B vitamins are water soluble, so excess amounts are excreted and hypervitaminosis is rare; inadequate levels are the larger concern.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vitamin B series is water soluble, and few aside from vitamin B12 are stored long term in the body. In contrast to the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K), the risk of hypervitaminosis from excess accumulation is rare because excess amounts are excreted. Inadequate B vitamin levels are a larger concern than overload.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Few B vitamins aside from B12 are stored long term; most become depleted without regular intake.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Accumulation with risk of hypervitaminosis characterizes the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, not the water-soluble B series.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding of cobalt is the mechanism by which nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin, not an effect of excess B vitamins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by the antifolate methotrexate, not by dietary folate.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 19-year-old refugee with severe malnutrition presents with dermatitis, fragile cracked skin at the corners of the lips, a swollen tongue, general fatigue, and diarrhea. Which of the following best explains why these particular tissues are affected in B vitamin deficiencies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are rapidly regenerating tissues dependent on DNA/RNA synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are the only tissues capable of synthesizing vitamins de novo

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are the primary sites of B vitamin absorption from the diet

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contain the highest concentrations of intrinsic factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: They store the majority of the body's B vitamins in flavoproteins

explanation.summary: B vitamin deficiencies share manifestations in rapidly growing or regenerating tissues because these vitamins are needed for energy production and DNA/RNA synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because B vitamins are required in reactions encompassing energy production and DNA/RNA synthesis, any vitamin B deficiency commonly impacts rapidly growing or regenerating tissues: skin and scalp (dermatitis), corners of the lips (cheilosis), lips (cheilitis), tongue (glossitis), general fatigue, and the gastrointestinal tract (diarrhea).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans, with rare exception, cannot synthesize vitamins de novo in any tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absorption occurs in the intestine (duodenum/jejunum for folate, terminal ileum for cobalamin), not in the skin or tongue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells; it is not concentrated in these tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin, lips, tongue, and gut are not B vitamin storage sites; B12 is stored in the liver and most others are not stored long term.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A public health team investigates a cluster of cheilosis, glossitis, and mild anemia in an impoverished community. Milk, a rich source of the deficient vitamin, is delivered to the community in transparent containers that sit in sunlight for hours. Which property of the vitamin best explains why this storage practice leads to deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is damaged by light

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is denatured by alcohol in the gut lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is destroyed by gastric acid unless bound to a carrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is rapidly excreted unless taken with fat

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires intrinsic factor for absorption

explanation.summary: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is damaged by light, so milk, a rich source, must not be stored in transparent containers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ariboflavinosis is most commonly caused by severe malnutrition in extremely impoverished areas, with additional cases observed when milk, a rich source of vitamin B2, is restricted or not properly stored. Because vitamin B2 is damaged by light, milk containers must not be transparent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alcohol denatures gastrointestinal proteins needed for absorption of B9/B12; it does not explain light-related loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction by acid and enzymes, requiring protective R-binders, describes cobalamin, not riboflavin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B vitamins are water soluble; fat is not required for their absorption, and this does not explain the storage issue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor is required for cobalamin absorption, and it is unrelated to light exposure of milk.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman from an impoverished region has cheilitis and a mild normocytic anemia. Her urinary riboflavin level is within the reference range, yet an erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity ratio (after riboflavin added/before riboflavin added) is 1.5. Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between the two tests?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ratio above 1.2 indicates riboflavin excess rather than deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: The activity ratio is elevated only in glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: The glutathione reductase assay measures pyridoxine rather than riboflavin status

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urine riboflavin reflects dietary intake but not the bioavailability within flavoproteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine riboflavin rises only after hepatic stores of the vitamin are exhausted

explanation.summary: Because bodily riboflavin is largely held within flavoproteins, a functional enzymatic assay is a better diagnostic than urine riboflavin, which measures intake only.
explanation.whyCorrect: Riboflavin is largely contained within flavoproteins as derivatives such as FMN or FAD. Simply measuring urine riboflavin provides a measure of dietary intake but fails to provide insight into bioavailability. An enzymatic assay of erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity in the absence and presence of exogenous riboflavin is therefore a better diagnostic; a ratio above 1.2 indicates ariboflavinosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A ratio above 1.2 indicates deficiency (ariboflavinosis), not excess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G6PD deficiency is a separate hemolytic anemia associated with the same pathway; it is not the reason the ratio rises in riboflavin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione reductase is a flavoprotein, so the assay reflects riboflavin, not pyridoxine, status.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Riboflavin is not stored long term in the liver; urine riboflavin simply tracks recent intake.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A medical student learns that riboflavin in the body is largely contained within a particular class of proteins that hold a riboflavin derivative. Which of the following is a prime example of this class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complex II of the electron transport chain, which uses FAD

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase, which reduces folate to FH4

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methionine synthase, which uses methyl-cobalamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The initial enzyme of porphyrin synthesis, which uses PLP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcobalamin II, which carries cobalamin in the blood

explanation.summary: Flavoproteins contain a riboflavin derivative such as FMN or FAD; Complex II of the ETC is a prime example.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bodily riboflavin is largely contained within flavoproteins, proteins that contain a riboflavin derivative such as FMN or FAD. Complex II of the electron transport chain is a prime example of a flavoprotein. Erythrocyte glutathione reductase, used to assess riboflavin status, is another.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dihydrofolate reductase acts on folate to generate tetrahydrofolate; it is not described as a flavoprotein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methionine synthase depends on methyl-cobalamin (vitamin B12), not a riboflavin derivative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The initial step of porphyrin synthesis uses pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, a vitamin B6 derivative.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transcobalamin II is a cobalamin transport protein in blood, not a flavoprotein.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A child with extremely severe, prolonged ariboflavinosis initially had a normocytic anemia. On repeat testing months later, the MCV has fallen below the reference range. Which of the following best explains this change in MCV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic bleeding from the gut has caused physical loss of morphologically normal red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutathione reductase failure has triggered hemolysis with a marked increase in red cell turnover

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency has progressed from mild to profound because riboflavin is needed for maximal iron absorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin deficiency has progressed far enough to impair DNA synthesis in marrow progenitors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Riboflavin deficiency has depleted pyridoxal 5'-phosphate and blocked the first step of porphyrin synthesis

explanation.summary: Vitamin B2 is required for maximal iron absorption; mild iron deficiency is normocytic, but severe iron deficiency becomes microcytic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B2 is required for maximal iron absorption, and iron is a required substrate for Hb. While mild iron deficiency presents as normocytic anemia, severe iron-deficient anemia is associated with microcytic anemia. A vitamin B2 deficient anemia is therefore normocytic unless extremely severe, at which point the MCV can fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Physical loss of normal cells causes normocytic anemia, not a drop in MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis with increased turnover would produce a normocytic picture; it does not explain a falling MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired DNA synthesis would raise the MCV (macrocytosis); it is the mechanism of folate/cobalamin deficiency, not riboflavin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PLP is a vitamin B6 derivative; riboflavin deficiency does not deplete PLP.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: The metabolic pathway whose enzyme activity is used to diagnose ariboflavinosis (erythrocyte glutathione reductase) is also associated with a common hemolytic anemia that is a separate but medically relevant feature of the same pathway. Which of the following is that disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate-deficiency macrocytic anemia of pregnancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isoniazid-associated microcytic anemia of B6 deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methotrexate-induced macrocytic megaloblastic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pernicious anemia from intrinsic factor loss

explanation.summary: The glutathione reductase pathway used to diagnose ariboflavinosis is also associated with G6PD deficiency, a common hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is critical for boards that the same metabolic pathway used for ariboflavinosis diagnosis (erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity) is also associated with a common hemolytic anemia known as glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. These are separate but medically relevant features of this pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate deficiency in pregnancy is a macrocytic anemia and is not linked to glutathione reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isoniazid lowers vitamin B6, impairing porphyrin synthesis; it is not a hemolytic anemia of this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate causes macrocytosis by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, not via the glutathione pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pernicious anemia is a macrocytic anemia from autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor/parietal cells, unrelated to the glutathione reductase pathway.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A dietitian notes that, among the B vitamins whose deficiency causes anemia, an isolated dietary deficiency of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is rare. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Humans synthesize pyridoxine de novo

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pyridoxine is protected from digestion by intrinsic factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine is regenerated from methyl-cobalamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxine is stored in the liver for several years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyridoxine is widely abundant in foods

explanation.summary: Vitamin B6 deficiency is rare because of its wide abundance in foods.
explanation.whyCorrect: A vitamin B6 deficiency is rare due to its wide abundance in foods. When deficiency does occur, it is often drug-related (e.g., isoniazid), and its active derivative pyridoxal 5'-phosphate is needed for the initial step of porphyrin synthesis, so deficiency yields microcytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: With rare exception, humans cannot synthesize vitamins; they can only modify the parent compound obtained from the diet.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrinsic factor protects and escorts cobalamin, not pyridoxine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methyl-cobalamin donates a methyl group to homocysteine; it has no role in regenerating pyridoxine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Long-term hepatic storage (years) is a feature of cobalamin, not pyridoxine; most B vitamins are not stored long term.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a 70-year-old man with macrocytic anemia is reviewed. One neutrophil displays 4 distinct nuclear lobes, while several others display 6 or more lobes. Which of the following is the correct interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both lobe counts fall within the normal range of variation for neutrophil nuclei

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 4-lobed cell is hypersegmented, since a normal neutrophil nucleus has no more than 3 lobes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 6-lobed cells are hypersegmented, reflecting suppressed DNA replication in these B9/B12-dependent cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 6-lobed cells indicate insufficient porphyrin synthesis from a pyridoxine deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 6-lobed cells reflect increased riboflavin availability within their flavoproteins

explanation.summary: Hypersegmented neutrophils have nuclei exceeding 5 lobes and result from suppressed DNA replication in folate/cobalamin deficiency; 4 lobes is within normal variation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils, phagocytic white blood cells of the innate immune system, are also dependent on vitamin B9 and vitamin B12 because they are rapidly dividing. Their multi-lobed nucleus normally shows about 4 lobes, which is within the normal range of variation. When DNA replication is suppressed, hypersegmented neutrophils with nuclei exceeding 5 lobes can occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nuclei exceeding 5 lobes are hypersegmented and abnormal, so the 6-lobed cells are not normal variation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A neutrophil with 4 distinct lobes is within the normal range of variation, not hypersegmented.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxine deficiency impairs porphyrin synthesis and causes microcytic anemia; it does not produce hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Riboflavin/flavoprotein status does not determine neutrophil nuclear lobulation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a folate deficiency has impaired nucleic acid synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Folate-derived one-carbon carriers are directly required for the synthesis of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenine, guanine, and thymidine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytosine and uracil only

choices.label: C
choices.text: FAD and FMN from riboflavin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porphyrin and heme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Succinyl-CoA from methylmalonyl-CoA

explanation.summary: Folate is required for synthesis of all purine bases (adenine and guanine) and the pyrimidine thymidine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate, after reduction to tetrahydrofolate (FH4), transfers one-carbon units needed for nucleic acid production. It is required for the synthesis of all purine nitrogenous bases (adenine and guanine) and the pyrimidine thymidine. Cobalamin is only indirectly required, via its role in cycling folate correctly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate's role in nitrogenous base synthesis covers the purines and thymidine, not cytosine and uracil alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FAD and FMN are riboflavin derivatives formed without folate involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porphyrin synthesis depends on pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6), not folate carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is a deoxyadenosyl-cobalamin (B12) reaction, independent of folate.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a long history of celiac disease, which has caused thickening of the intestinal lining around the jejunum, has had multiple severe flares over the past 9 months despite adherence to a gluten-free diet. Laboratory workup shows a macrocytic anemia, elevated homocysteine, and methylmalonic acid within the reference range. There are no neurologic deficits. Which of the following deficiencies best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin, absorbed in the terminal ileum rather than the jejunum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cobalamin, protected by R-binders in the stomach

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate, absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxine, required for the initial step of porphyrin synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Riboflavin, carried within erythrocyte flavoproteins

explanation.summary: Jejunal damage with macrocytosis, elevated homocysteine, and normal MMA points to a primary folate deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate is absorbed from the diet in the proximal intestine within the duodenum and jejunum, so damage to the jejunum from celiac flares impairs its uptake. GI damage from inflammatory diseases such as Crohn's and celiac is a listed cause of folate deficiency. MMA within the reference range rules out a vitamin B12 problem, while elevated homocysteine and macrocytosis are consistent with folate deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin deficiency would elevate MMA, which is normal here, and the damaged region (jejunum) is not the ileal absorption site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: R-binders protect cobalamin from gastric acid, but the normal MMA excludes a cobalamin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxine deficiency produces microcytic anemia from insufficient porphyrin, not a macrocytic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Riboflavin deficiency causes a normocytic anemia, not macrocytosis with elevated homocysteine.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: Vitamin B12's structure is damaged by digestive processes such as acid and enzymes. Within the stomach, which of the following is damaged by the harsh environment in place of vitamin B12, thereby preserving the vitamin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intrinsic factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pancreatic proteases

choices.label: D
choices.text: R-binders

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcobalamin II

explanation.summary: Gastric mucosa cells secrete R-binders, protective escort proteins that are damaged by the stomach's environment instead of vitamin B12.
explanation.whyCorrect: To ensure vitamin B12 is preserved, gastric mucosa cells secrete protective proteins known as R-binders. This escort protein is damaged by the stomach's harsh environment instead of vitamin B12. Intrinsic factor, secreted by parietal cells, then facilitates cobalamin's transit through the small intestine to the terminal ileum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces folate to FH4 and has no role in cobalamin protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrinsic factor facilitates transit through the small intestine and protects B12 from pancreatic enzymes; it is not the gastric escort sacrificed to acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic proteases act in the small intestine and are digestive enzymes, not protective escorts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transcobalamin II carries cobalamin in the blood after ileal absorption, not within the stomach.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: Dietary cobalamin leaves the stomach bound to its gastric escort protein. In the small intestine it must be released from this escort so that it can bind intrinsic factor and travel to the terminal ileum. Which of the following accomplishes this release?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocyte glutathione reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastric acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreatic proteases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcobalamin II

explanation.summary: Pancreatic proteases degrade the R-binder in the small intestine, freeing cobalamin to bind intrinsic factor for transit to the terminal ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the absorption pathway of dietary cobalamin, R-binders protect B12 in the stomach; in the small intestine, proteases from the pancreas act on the R-binder complex so cobalamin can transfer to intrinsic factor. IF then ensures that vitamin B12 is not degraded by the digestive pancreatic enzymes and escorts it to the terminal ileum for absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces folate; it has no role in cobalamin absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocyte glutathione reductase is a flavoprotein used to assess riboflavin status, unrelated to B12 absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric acid acts in the stomach to denature dietary proteins and activate stomach proteases; it does not free B12 from R-binders in the intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transcobalamin II binds cobalamin in the blood after absorption, not in the intestinal lumen.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: After absorption in the terminal ileum, cobalamin enters the bloodstream. Which of the following best describes its transport and distribution in the body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bound to flavoproteins, with roughly half delivered to muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bound to intrinsic factor, with nearly all delivered to bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bound to R-binders, with nearly all delivered to the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bound to transcobalamin II, with roughly half delivered to the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free in plasma, with roughly half excreted in urine within a day

explanation.summary: Absorbed cobalamin circulates bound to transcobalamin II, with about 50% going to hepatic stores and about 50% to other tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once absorbed from the ileum, cobalamin is carried in the blood by transcobalamin II. Approximately 50% is delivered to the liver, where the average individual stores sufficient cobalamin for several years, and approximately 50% is delivered to other tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flavoproteins contain riboflavin derivatives; they do not transport cobalamin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrinsic factor escorts B12 through the small intestine to the ileum; it is not the blood carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.C: R-binders protect B12 within the stomach; they do not transport it in blood, and only about half goes to the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cobalamin is not carried free and is stored for years rather than rapidly excreted.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has taken a proton pump inhibitor at high doses for many years. He develops a macrocytic anemia with elevated methylmalonic acid and elevated homocysteine. Which of the following best explains his vitamin B12 deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acid is needed to denature dietary proteins and activate stomach proteases that release B12

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug binds the cobalt ion of cobalamin, rendering the vitamin inert

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug damages the terminal ileum so that IF-bound B12 cannot be absorbed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug induces autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, trapping folate as methyl-FH4

explanation.summary: Excess proton pump inhibitor use leaves most vitamin B12 bound to dietary proteins because gastric acid is required to denature those proteins and activate stomach proteases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proton pump inhibitors, taken in excess, leave the majority of vitamin B12 bound to dietary proteins. Acid is needed both to denature these proteins and to activate stomach proteases that degrade protein to release vitamin B12. Aggressive antacid intake is listed as a less common cause of B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding the cobalt ion is the mechanism of nitrous oxide (laughing gas), not of proton pump inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proton pump inhibitors act in the stomach on acid production; the brick does not describe ileal damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoantibodies against parietal cells and/or IF define pernicious anemia, an autoimmune disease, not a drug effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of DHFR is the mechanism of the antifolate methotrexate and would impair folate, not B12.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Metabolic Overview III - O2 Delivery (2 of 2): Anemia, MCV Classification, and the B Vitamins

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is found to have a macrocytic anemia, and testing reveals autoantibodies directed against gastric parietal cells. Which of the following statements about her condition is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It develops within weeks because the deficient vitamin has no true body stores

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is autoimmune, disproportionately affects women, and most cases occur after age 60

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is most commonly caused by severe malnutrition in impoverished regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is rare because the deficient vitamin is widely abundant in foods

choices.label: E
choices.text: It results from light-induced destruction of the vitamin in stored milk

explanation.summary: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune cause of cobalamin deficiency that disproportionately affects women, with most cases after age 60.
explanation.whyCorrect: In pernicious anemia, autoantibodies against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor compromise the ability to absorb dietary vitamin B12, producing a macrocytic anemia. Historically patients continually declined until death (hence 'pernicious'). As an autoimmune disease, it can disproportionately affect women compared to men, and it has an age component with most cases occurring after the age of 60.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lack of true stores (weeks to months) describes folate; cobalamin is stored in the liver for years, so deficiency develops slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Severe malnutrition is the most common cause of ariboflavinosis (vitamin B2 deficiency), not pernicious anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wide abundance in foods explains why vitamin B6 deficiency is rare; pernicious anemia reflects malabsorption, not intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Light damages riboflavin in milk; it has nothing to do with autoimmune B12 malabsorption.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a vitamin B12 deficiency and adequate dietary folate intake develops a macrocytic anemia. Cobalamin is not directly involved in the synthetic cascades of nitrogenous bases. Which of the following best explains why his anemia develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin deficiency causes folate to be excreted before it can reach the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cobalamin deficiency damages the duodenum and jejunum, so dietary folate is not absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cobalamin deficiency inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so dietary folate is never reduced to FH4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cobalamin is directly required as the coenzyme for thymidine and purine synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methyl-FH4 can donate its methyl group only to cobalamin, so it accumulates and FH4 is not regenerated

explanation.summary: In cobalamin deficiency, methyl-FH4 becomes trapped because its only acceptor is cobalamin, so FH4 cannot be recycled for nucleic acid synthesis (the methyl trap).
explanation.whyCorrect: When methyl-FH4 is formed it can only donate its methyl group to cobalamin, and this donation regenerates FH4 to continue one-carbon transfers. A cobalamin deficiency alone therefore causes methyl-FH4 to accumulate and be trapped, preventing regeneration and recycling of FH4 and leading to macrocytic anemia even with adequate folate. This scenario can be erroneously diagnosed as a primary folate deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The problem is trapping of folate as methyl-FH4, not accelerated excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cobalamin deficiency does not damage the proximal intestine or block folate absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cobalamin does not act on dihydrofolate reductase; DHFR is inhibited by methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cobalamin is only indirectly required for nitrogenous base synthesis; folate carriers are the direct participants.

questions.stem: Vitamin B12 participates in only two reactions in the human body, with its cobalt coordinating one of two reactant groups. Which of the following describes the cobalamin function that occurs completely independent of folate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Connection of carbon skeletons to the TCA cycle via deoxyadenosine-cobalamin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donation of a methyl group to homocysteine to form methionine via methyl-cobalamin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduction of dietary folate to tetrahydrofolate via dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regeneration of FH4 from methyl-FH4 via the methyl-cobalamin cofactor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfer of one-carbon units for purine ring synthesis via FH4 derivatives

explanation.summary: Deoxyadenosine-cobalamin connects carbon skeletons back into the TCA cycle, a function of B12 that is completely independent of folate and whose failure elevates MMA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 is involved in only two reactions. Methyl-cobalamin accepts the methyl group from methyl-FH4 (regenerating FH4) and donates it to homocysteine to produce methionine, a folate-linked process. Deoxyadenosine-cobalamin ultimately connects various carbon skeletons back into the TCA cycle so they can be oxidized; unlike methyl-cobalamin, this function occurs completely independent of folate, and its failure produces the elevated MMA that helps confirm B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Methyl donation to homocysteine (forming methionine) uses the methyl group derived from methyl-FH4, so it is folate-dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduction of folate by DHFR is a folate modification that does not involve cobalamin at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regeneration of FH4 from methyl-FH4 is the methyl-cobalamin reaction, which is intimately linked to folate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: One-carbon transfers for purine synthesis are folate (FH4) reactions, not a cobalamin function.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 6-year history of heavy alcohol use has a macrocytic anemia, new changes in gait, and a 'pins and needles' sensation in both feet. Serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both elevated. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated MMA indicates folate deficiency, so vitamin B12 status is irrelevant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate deficiency is confirmed, and vitamin B12 deficiency is ruled out

choices.label: C
choices.text: The neurologic findings indicate folate deficiency rather than vitamin B12 deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency is confirmed, but a coexisting folate deficiency is not ruled out

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency is ruled out because homocysteine is elevated

explanation.summary: Neurologic deficits and elevated MMA confirm that vitamin B12 is lacking, but they do NOT rule out a folate deficiency, which is common in chronic alcohol use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 deficiency alone causes elevated MMA and leads to neurological deficits such as changes in gait and peripheral neuropathy (paresthesia). If these are positive in a patient, it does not rule out a folate deficiency; it merely confirms that vitamin B12 is lacking. Chronic alcohol use is a common factor producing co-deficiencies in vitamin B9 and B12, and elevated homocysteine is shared by both.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated MMA is unique to B12 deficiency; it says nothing about folate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated MMA and neuropathy confirm B12 deficiency; nothing here rules it out.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral neuropathy is unique to B12 deficiency, not a feature of folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homocysteine is elevated in both folate and B12 deficiency, so it cannot exclude B12 deficiency.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has followed a diet that excludes all meat, fish, eggs, and dairy for the past 5 years. Which of the following supplementation strategies best addresses the nutritional risk created by this dietary practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin from fortified yeast spread or fortified cereal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate from leafy green vegetables, nuts, and chickpeas

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine from a wider variety of plant-based whole foods

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin from fortified milk stored in opaque containers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine from enriched whole grains, nuts, and legumes

explanation.summary: Diets restricting meat need to ensure vitamin B12 intake through supplementation or fortified sources such as yeast spread or cereal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common dietary sources of cobalamin are meat including fish, eggs, dairy (milk, yogurt), and fortified sources such as cereal. Diets restricting meat therefore need to ensure proper vitamin B12 intake through supplementation or addition of rich sources such as fortified yeast spread. Inadequate dietary intake from select dietary practices is a listed cause of B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate comes from fruits, leafy greens, nuts/seeds, whole grains, and chickpeas, which this diet does not exclude.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine is widely abundant in foods, so a meat-free diet does not create a specific B6 risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Milk is excluded by her diet and is a riboflavin source; the vitamin uniquely at risk when animal products are excluded is B12.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine is not a vitamin linked to anemia in this context and is not the deficiency created by excluding animal products.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in early pregnancy asks which vitamin she should be most careful to obtain, having heard that its deficiency is linked to neural tube defects and that pregnancy increases the demand for it. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is she describing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate (B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine (B6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin (B2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine (B1)

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency in pregnancy is associated with neural tube defects, and pregnancy increases folate demand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the deficiency symptoms listed for folate (B9) are macrocytic anemia and, in pregnancy, neural tube defects. Pregnancy (increased demand) is also a listed cause of folate deficiency. Because folate has no true stores (estimated to last weeks to months), adequate intake is essential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin deficiency is uniquely linked to peripheral neuropathy and elevated MMA, not neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia via impaired porphyrin synthesis, not neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency causes a normocytic anemia and is not linked to neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine is excluded from the anemia differential and is not the vitamin associated with neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man undergoes gastric bypass surgery, after which he can no longer absorb dietary cobalamin. Assuming his stores were adequate before surgery, approximately how long would his hepatic cobalamin stores be expected to last?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A few days

choices.label: B
choices.text: More than 20 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roughly 12 to 18 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Roughly 3 to 6 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weeks to months

explanation.summary: The liver stores enough cobalamin to last several years, so B12 deficiency develops slowly after absorption is lost.
explanation.whyCorrect: The average individual stores sufficient cobalamin in the liver for several years (described as 3-6 years in the text and 4-6 years in the comparison table). Gastric bypass surgery is a listed GI structural change that impedes B9 and B12 absorption, but because of these hepatic stores, B12 deficiency generally appears later than folate deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No B vitamin relevant here is depleted within days; even folate lasts weeks to months.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stores do not last decades; a multi-year window such as the 4 years of heavy drinking in the case is sufficient to deplete them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 12- to 18-month window underestimates hepatic cobalamin stores, which last several years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weeks to months is the estimate for folate, which has no true stores, not for cobalamin.
